rh-l1q2.summary: On Lombard's first distinction, Holcot asks whether the created will is free with freedom of contradiction in using and enjoying. He answers yes, after a long series of principal arguments built from sophismata, insolubilia, and paradoxes of instants and infinity. He criticizes Anselm's definition of freedom as power to keep rectitude and his affections of the will as superfluous. Freedom is the will itself under various connotations, and freedom of contradiction is the power, given all requisites, to act or not. That power is understood diachronically, as power immediately before the act, with composite and divided senses distinguished. Rectitude is conformity to divine law and may consist in willing nothing. The will is active and passive, a partial cause alongside cognition. Volition is an optative mental sentence, delight is distinct from volition, and volition is produced successively without a first instant. The created will can be necessitated by extreme objects, habit, complexion, grace, or temptation, and most human acts are free only interpretatively, yet no one is necessitated to sin. Love can exist without an object. Free agents need no new disposition to act, against Averroes and the eternity of motion. Paradoxical obligations and perplexity cases are resolved through the logic of obligations, conditions, and divine dispensation.
claims: The created will is free with freedom of contradiction.
Freedom is the will itself under different connotations.
Freedom of contradiction is diachronic power immediately before acting.
Volition is an optative mental sentence produced successively.
The will can be necessitated, but no one is necessitated to sin.
Love can exist without an existing object.

rh-l1q2-Dd1e101.summary: Opening statement of the question on Lombard's first distinction: whether the created will, in using and enjoying, is free with freedom of contradiction.

rh-l1q2-d1e108.summary: States the question, on Lombard's first distinction concerning use and enjoyment: whether the created will, in using and enjoying, is free with freedom of contradiction.

rh-l1q2-Dd1e103.summary: Fourteen principal arguments, many built on sophismata and insolubilia, attack the freedom of contradiction. Freely willing or not willing, and suspending every act, seem self-contradictory. The will seems unable to cut off intellection. Self-referential dictates of reason make conformity or nonconformity contradictory. Conditional promises, manumissions, vows, marriages, and a divinely sanctioned liar case generate paradoxes. Circular loves are inconsistent. Free consideration requires prior consideration. Anselm requires prior willing for any self-motion. Proportional alternation of merit and sin, intensification, and comparisons of malice yield infinite or indeterminate reward and guilt. Volition seems instantaneous, supported by seventeen sub-arguments about Christ, the Eucharist, illumination, angels, and first and last instants. Averroes makes contingency passive. God clearly seen seems to necessitate love. Avoiding sin seems impossible, and perplexity cases seem to force sin. Virtuous penance seems to require contrary emotions. For the opposite stand Aristotle, Augustine, Anselm, and Bernard.
claims: Freedom of contradiction appears to generate contradictions, insolubilia, and paradoxes of merit and time.

rh-l1q2-d1e121.summary: First principal argument: the will cannot freely will and freely not will. 'The will freely wills' is impossible, since while it actually wills it is not in potency of contradiction to that act, as whatever is in potency to an act lacks it. By parity 'a man freely understands' or 'speaks' would be possible, which is false.
claims: 'The will freely wills' is impossible, since actual willing excludes potency to the opposite.

rh-l1q2-d1e176.summary: Further: if the will could freely will, its future volitions would be in its power, since Lombard says free choice concerns only the future. But if Socrates can love Plato a hundred times a day with equal acts, all are equally in his power and he could no more cause one than another, so either all or none would be produced.
claims: Equally available volitions give no reason to produce one rather than another.

rh-l1q2-d1e215.summary: Further: any act in the will's power is either one that exists, which it cannot now cause, or one that does not, which as nothing is in no one's power.
claims: Neither existing nor nonexistent acts are in the will's power.

rh-l1q2-d1e232.summary: Proves that the will cannot freely not will. Whatever is free is voluntary, so freely not willing is voluntarily not willing, i.e. not willing by willing, so willing and not willing at once, a contradiction.
claims: Freely not willing implies willing and not willing at once.

rh-l1q2-d1e269.summary: Second principal argument. A free will could freely suspend every act, since, per Augustine, nothing is more in the will's power than the will itself. But freely suspending every act means willing to suspend, so having an act, so not suspending every act, a contradiction.
claims: Freely suspending all acts of will is self-contradictory.

rh-l1q2-d1e320.summary: Third principal argument. A free will could cut off any intellection, since Augustine calls the will queen of the soul and Anselm says it moves all instruments, including intellect, without resistance.
claims: According to Augustine and Anselm, the will rules the intellect and can halt its acts.
concepts: will as queen of the soul

rh-l1q2-d1e353.summary: Supports this from Aristotle: recollection is a bodily passion because it does not obey the will, so the incorporeal intellect obeys the will and can be used at will.
claims: According to Aristotle, the immaterial intellect obeys the will.

rh-l1q2-d1e375.summary: Further, from Metaphysics IX: irrational powers act as soon as agent and patient are disposed and impediments are removed, but rational powers additionally require will or choice. So the intellect's act can be impeded by the will as well as by the absence of species or object.
claims: According to Aristotle, rational powers require the will's concurrence to act.

rh-l1q2-d1e425.summary: Further: Augustine (De trinitate) holds that the will joins parent and offspring in forming cognition, so there is no actual cognition without the will. The consequent, that the will can cut off any intellection, is then shown false in several ways.
claims: According to Augustine, the will is required to form actual cognition.

rh-l1q2-d1e448.summary: First disproof: then someone burning in fire could freely cut off his awareness of the burning. To the reply that sense is necessitated by its objects, see below.
claims: The will cannot stop awareness of intense pain.

rh-l1q2-d1e464.summary: Against that reply: can the will cut off the intellectual awareness of the pain? If so, a man could understand himself not to be in pain.
claims: If the will could cut off awareness of pain, one could judge oneself painless.

rh-l1q2-d1e473.summary: Further: when external sense acts and imagination is unimpeded, intellection of the same object is necessarily caused, as experience shows.
claims: Sensation with unimpeded imagination necessarily causes intellection.

rh-l1q2-d1e484.summary: Further: the will's power to cut off intellection of an object a is finite. If a's power is less, the will exceeds it by a finite excess, so God could create an object b exceeding a by that excess, equal to the will's power. The will could not interrupt intellection of b.
claims: Some object could have power to sustain intellection equal to the will's power to stop it.

rh-l1q2-d1e534.summary: Fourth principal argument: the will cannot freely will against every judgment of reason and also conform to every judgment. If reason dictates a, 'you ought to will against every judgment', then willing against every judgment means both conforming and not conforming to a.
claims: A self-referential dictate makes willing against every judgment contradictory.

rh-l1q2-d1e598.summary: Proves the will cannot conform to every judgment: if reason dictates willing nothing before tomorrow, conforming means willing to conform, so willing something before tomorrow, so not conforming.
claims: A dictate to will nothing cannot be conformed to by willing.

rh-l1q2-d1e623.summary: A reply: one conforms to that judgment by not willing, since it concerns not-willing, so 'conforms, so wills conformably' does not follow.
claims: One can conform to a dictate of not-willing by not willing.

rh-l1q2-d1e636.summary: Against that reply: if God gave that dictate as a precept, the will conforming by willing nothing would be right and meritorious without willing what God wills it to will, so Anselm's definition of rectitude as willing what God wills one to will is wrong.
claims: Conformity by not willing refutes Anselm's definition of rectitude.

rh-l1q2-d1e671.summary: Further: if reason dictates that Socrates should rather will Plato damned than sin mortally himself, and he conforms, then since willing Plato damned is itself mortal sin, he would will Plato damned more than he wills Plato damned, a contradiction.
claims: Preferring another's damnation to one's own sin yields contradiction.

rh-l1q2-d1e721.summary: Further: unless judgment necessitates the will, one could sin mortally without an act of will. If one judges one should help a needy person and suspends one's will, he shuts his heart and sins mortally, yet without an act, against Augustine's 'sin is so voluntary that unless voluntary it is not sin'.
claims: If the will can suspend against judgment, sin without an act of will is possible.

rh-l1q2-d1e758.summary: Further: with a clearest judgment about something to be done, if the will can will the opposite, the opposite must appear good, so one would hold contrary judgments, one maximally. And if reason dictates willing God's honor more than one's own advantage, conforming means willing a more than a. Fifth principal argument: a free will can bind itself by conditional promise and is bound when the condition holds, as the saying 'every promise of the faithful is a debt' and canon law (De iureiurando) attest.
claims: The will cannot act against a clearest judgment without contrary judgments.
A conditional promise binds when the condition is fulfilled.

rh-l1q2-d1e833.summary: Shows the claim about conditional obligation is false by a paradox. Socrates binds himself to give Plato ten if at instant a Plato meets only a man who is not bound to him. If Plato meets only Socrates, then if Socrates is bound he is not, and if not, he is.
claims: A self-referential conditional obligation makes the debtor bound if and only if not bound.

rh-l1q2-d1e886.summary: Further: Socrates binds himself to Cicero for twenty if Plato binds himself immediately after; Plato binds himself for ten if Socrates owes nothing. Then if Plato is bound he is not, and if not he is.
claims: Mutually dependent conditional obligations yield paradox.

rh-l1q2-d1e928.summary: Further: a master frees his slaves Socrates and Plato each on condition that the first he meets is not free; when they meet each other, neither can consistently be free.
claims: Conditional manumission can be paradoxical.

rh-l1q2-d1e965.summary: Further: Peter wills to enter religion if John does, and John if Peter does not. Then Peter wills to enter if and only if he does not, so not everyone who wills something under a condition wills it when the condition holds.
claims: Conditional volitions can be paradoxical.

rh-l1q2-d1e1009.summary: Further: Martin and Bertha marry by words of present consent, each on condition that the other speak truly immediately after instant a. Each then says 'you are not my spouse'. If the contract holds, both spoke truly, so neither is spouse; if not, both spoke truly, so it holds.
claims: A conditional marriage contract can be paradoxical.

rh-l1q2-d1e1059.summary: Further: God commands Socrates to avoid all falsehood, permits everything else, and certifies that if he speaks falsely he will be damned. Socrates then says only 'Socrates will be damned'. If he is justly damned he spoke truly, so should not be; if not, he spoke falsely, so should be.
claims: A divinely sanctioned liar case makes damnation paradoxical.

rh-l1q2-d1e1100.summary: Sixth principal argument: if each will is free, one could love and not love another at once. With only Socrates, Plato, and Cicero, Socrates loves whoever loves him, Plato loves only Socrates, and Cicero loves Socrates if Socrates loves only one man. Then Socrates loves only Plato if and only if he does not.
claims: Free mutual love among three can generate contradiction.

rh-l1q2-d1e1158.summary: Further: if Socrates is white and Plato black, and each wills to be like the other's color, Socrates wills to be like Plato and not like Plato.
claims: Wills about similarity can conflict.

rh-l1q2-d1e1184.summary: Seventh principal argument: one could use acquired science and consider at will, as Averroes says a habit allows considering whenever one wishes. But if Socrates freely now considers a, he first willed to consider a, and since what is willed is known, he considered a before considering a.
claims: Freely beginning to consider something requires prior consideration of it.

rh-l1q2-d1e1265.summary: Proves the last inference: willing a requires thinking of a, as Anselm distinguishes the will as instrument from its use, which occurs only when the willed thing is thought of. So willing to consider a presupposes considering a.
claims: Actual willing requires thinking of the object.

rh-l1q2-d1e1294.summary: Further: one could freely recall what is in memory, but willing to recall a proceeds from recalling a (Augustine: whatever we will to recall we have already recalled), so the same would be cause and effect.
claims: According to Augustine, willing to recall presupposes recalling.

rh-l1q2-d1e1325.summary: Further: a free act requires prior deliberation, so before considering a one would deliberate whether to consider a, which is already considering it.
claims: Deliberating whether to consider presupposes considering.

rh-l1q2-d1e1352.summary: Further: the will could freely divert the intellect from a to an unconsidered b, but willing to consider b requires already considering b.
claims: Willing to turn to an unconsidered object is impossible.

rh-l1q2-d1e1388.summary: Eighth principal argument: the will cannot elicit opposite acts successively and immediately. If an angel wills Socrates sitting through hour a and not sitting through hour b, then by Anselm whatever moves itself to will first wills so to move, so before b it willed Socrates not sitting while willing him sitting.
claims: According to Anselm, self-movement to will requires prior willing, so immediate succession of opposite volitions is impossible.

rh-l1q2-d1e1432.summary: Ninth principal argument: the will could freely merit and demerit at once, which is shown false in several ways.

rh-l1q2-d1e1443.summary: First: if someone merits and sins in alternating proportional parts of an hour and dies at its end a, he was neither finally good nor finally bad, so God could neither reward nor punish him, since any interval before a contains both.
claims: Alternating merit and sin over proportional parts leaves no final state.

rh-l1q2-d1e1491.summary: Further: if Socrates intensifies a meritorious act until he dies at a, there is no maximum degree of merit he had, so God could not reward him fittingly according to his highest degree.
claims: Continuous intensification leaves no maximum merit to reward.

rh-l1q2-d1e1513.summary: Further: Socrates and Plato merit equally for an hour; Socrates dies at its end a, Plato lives on without further merit. If Plato gets more for the instant a, either an indivisible reward corresponds to an instant, so infinite instants deserve infinite reward, or a divisible one, which can be matched by merit over time, so instantaneous and temporal merit would be equal.
claims: Rewarding the final instant leads to paradox about instantaneous merit.

rh-l1q2-d1e1592.summary: Further: a good end diminishes sin. If Plato kills his father for the republic's good and Socrates for no end, Socrates sins more than twice, thrice, fourfold, and so on as gravely, so with infinite intensive malice.
claims: Comparing sins with and without good ends implies infinite malice.

rh-l1q2-d1e1658.summary: Further: willing to kill two is of some gravity, four of fourfold, so willing to kill infinitely many is of infinite malice.
claims: Willing infinitely many killings would be of infinite malice.

rh-l1q2-d1e1671.summary: Further: willing to sin for two days is graver than for one, so willing to sin for infinite time is infinitely graver.
claims: Willing to sin forever is infinitely grave.

rh-l1q2-d1e1687.summary: Further: if willing to sin forever were graver than for one day only by a fixed proportion, say a hundredfold, some finite number of days would reach that proportion, and willing to sin forever would be no graver than that.
claims: Willing to sin forever cannot be graver by only a finite proportion.

rh-l1q2-d1e1735.summary: Further: drunkenness is a sin of infinite gravity, since infinite evils could follow, and the drunkard sins no less if they do not, having caused them as far as he can. Aristotle says the drunkard deserves double blame, for drunkenness and for what he does in ignorance.
claims: Drunkenness would be of infinite gravity through its potential consequences.

rh-l1q2-d1e1777.summary: Further: Socrates swears to reveal to Plato every sin he commits before a, then gets drunk and does not reveal it. He is perjured, which is a second unrevealed sin, so perjured again, and so to infinity, sinning infinitely and meriting infinite punishment.
claims: A self-referential oath generates infinite perjuries.

rh-l1q2-d1e1820.summary: Tenth principal argument: a free will could act in an instant or over time as it pleased. But nothing resists it, so action follows at once (Averroes on Physics IV).
claims: The will acts instantly since it meets no resistance.

rh-l1q2-d1e1836.summary: Further: if the will could only will anew over time, a sinner would necessarily remain in sin for some time before contrition, willy-nilly.
claims: If volition takes time, a sinner remains in sin necessarily for a time.

rh-l1q2-d1e1849.summary: Further: otherwise Christ did not merit at the first instant of his conception, against Lombard (III d. 18), who says he had supreme merit from the beginning.
claims: According to Lombard, Christ merited from the first instant of conception.

rh-l1q2-d1e1868.summary: Further: otherwise Christ would not be suddenly present on the altar, since if he is there by willing and can will only over time, he would be there before willing it or will it before being there.
claims: Eucharistic presence requires instantaneous volition.

rh-l1q2-d1e1884.summary: Further: a free power is as strong as a natural one, and natural powers act instantly, as a luminous body illuminates at once. Augustine: the will is present without interval as soon as we will.
claims: Free powers can act instantly as natural ones do.

rh-l1q2-d1e1906.summary: Further: the intellect understands instantly (Aristotle and Averroes, De anima III: intellection is a perfect act in no time), so the will, equally active and immaterial, can will instantly.
claims: According to Aristotle and Averroes, intellection is instantaneous, so volition can be too.

rh-l1q2-d1e1925.summary: Further: per Metaphysics XII, delight follows apprehension like a shadow, and delight involves volition, so volition follows apprehension in the same measure.
claims: Volition follows apprehension immediately.

rh-l1q2-d1e1936.summary: Further: vision occurs instantly (Averroes: sensing is a perfect act without time), so volition does too.
claims: Sensation is instantaneous, so volition is.

rh-l1q2-d1e1954.summary: Confirmation: whenever an animal sees, the will joins the visual power to its object (Augustine, De trinitate), and only by its act, so if vision is instantaneous so is volition.
claims: The will's act joins sense to object in every perception.

rh-l1q2-d1e1972.summary: Further: some natural agents act instantly, like a luminous body, so the will much more.
claims: Natural agents act instantly, so the will can.

rh-l1q2-d1e1983.summary: Further: if volition takes time, the devil sinned only when already obdurate and so never freely. Had his bad volition lasted through time without a first instant, he could have repented in the second part; if sin did not precede obduracy, no fault preceded punishment, against Augustine.
claims: The devil's sin requires an instantaneous volition.

rh-l1q2-d1e2025.summary: Further: without a first instant of volition there is no last either, so between the first angel's demerit and punishment there would be an instant when he was neither blessed nor wretched, against Augustine, who says sin is never without its fitting punishment for any interval.
claims: Augustine denies any interval between sin and punishment.

rh-l1q2-d1e2063.summary: Further: per Augustine the devil's sin was never without punishment, so without a first instant of sin, sin would not precede its punishment, yet an efficient cause precedes its effect in time (Averroes).
claims: Sin must precede its punishment in time.

rh-l1q2-d1e2083.summary: Further: without a first instant there would be a last instant of charity, so a permanent thing being corrupted would exist at the middle instant between being and non-being, against Aristotle and Averroes (Physics VIII).
claims: A permanent thing does not exist at the transition instant of its corruption.

rh-l1q2-d1e2103.summary: Further: if commanded to begin a meritorious work at an instant and one omits it, one did not sin at that instant (no volition was yet required) nor after (the command was not for after), so one sinned and did not sin.
claims: Commands to begin at an instant make omission paradoxical.

rh-l1q2-d1e2134.summary: Further: then a permanent thing could last only an instant, as if God created charity in someone who immediately sinned mortally, contrary to Aristotle, who says what exists in act exists in time.
claims: A permanent thing cannot last only an instant.

rh-l1q2-d1e2168.summary: Further: the angel knew and praised God as soon as created, so had an act of will at the first instant.
claims: Angels willed at the first instant of creation.

rh-l1q2-d1e2177.summary: Further: without a first instant of volition an angel could sin at creation without first being good, against Augustine (City of God XII), who argues no will can be evil from the start since vice removes a prior good.
claims: According to Augustine, an evil will presupposes a prior good.

rh-l1q2-d1e2207.summary: Eleventh principal argument: a free will would be passive, not active. Averroes says contingency ad utrumlibet is found not in per se agents but in passive powers. But a passive power suffers necessarily when the agents are present, so freedom would perish.
claims: According to Averroes, contingency to either side belongs to passive powers.

rh-l1q2-d1e2255.summary: Twelfth principal argument: a free will could freely not love God clearly seen, against Lombard (IV), who says Christ's deity cannot be seen without joy. But if the will necessarily loves God seen, per Augustine it would not be a will, since a will not in our power is not free or a will. Also it could not-will beatitude, against Augustine's 'all men will to live happily'.
claims: According to Lombard, God clearly seen cannot be seen without joy.
According to Augustine, a necessary volition would not be a will.

rh-l1q2-d1e2325.summary: Thirteenth principal argument: a created will cannot freely avoid sin. Adam could not avoid sin when he sinned (it was not then future) or after (the past cannot be undone), so only in a time a before. Then he was bound to avoid it only in a, so after a he did not sin.
claims: Adam could avoid sin only before sinning, so was obliged only then.

rh-l1q2-d1e2362.summary: Further: one can avoid only a future sin. But a future sin was future from eternity, and to prevent it would be to deceive God or Christ's soul, who assented to its being future.
claims: Avoiding a future sin would falsify God's foreknowledge.

rh-l1q2-d1e2393.summary: Further: if the will avoided sin a, it did not commit a, so a was not future, so it did not avoid a future sin.
claims: An avoided sin was never future.

rh-l1q2-d1e2412.summary: Further: is one bound to avoid a sin one will commit, or one not committed? Not the latter, since one cannot avoid what one never commits.
claims: One cannot avoid a sin one never commits.

rh-l1q2-d1e2426.summary: If bound to avoid a sin one will commit, one is bound to the impossible, since 'whatever is to be committed by oneself is to be committed by oneself' is necessary.
claims: Being bound to avoid what one will commit is being bound to the impossible.

rh-l1q2-d1e2435.summary: Further: in a possible case the will is necessitated to sin. God reveals to Socrates in charity that, of Socrates and Plato, only the one who sins mortally tomorrow will be saved. If Socrates now wills to sin tomorrow he sins now; if not, he wills not to be saved and so lacks charity and sins.
claims: A revelation can leave one no sinless option.

rh-l1q2-d1e2479.summary: Further: if God reveals that Socrates will be saved only by murdering Plato, he must either not will his salvation or will the murder, against Augustine's 'sin is so voluntary'.
claims: Salvation conditional on murder forces sin.

rh-l1q2-d1e2497.summary: Further: whoever consents to mortal sin sins mortally, yet one can be perplexed between two sins and is bound to choose the lesser (Decretum d. 13, 'duo mala'), so sometimes bound to sin.
claims: Perplexity between two sins forces sinning.

rh-l1q2-d1e2523.summary: Further: if someone will kill you unless you consent to his mortal sin, consenting is sin, and refusing means preferring that he kill you, so consenting to his sin.
claims: Coercion can leave no sinless option.

rh-l1q2-d1e2539.summary: Further: a master knows his servant will fornicate if he goes out and fornicate and murder if he stays, and he cannot prevent it, so he is necessitated to sin.
claims: Foreseeing unavoidable sins of others necessitates sin.

rh-l1q2-d1e2560.summary: Further: a judge who privately knows a secret marriage was contracted, but sees the opposite legally proved, either grants divorce and consents to sin, or does justice against the evidence and causes scandal and disrepute.
claims: A judge with private knowledge faces a sinful choice.

rh-l1q2-d1e2582.summary: Further: someone in extreme need who can borrow only from a usurer either consents to usury or causes his own death.
claims: Extreme need can force consent to usury.

rh-l1q2-d1e2600.summary: Further: Socrates and Plato, equally strong, in extreme need, equidistant from a loaf that can save only one. If both strive, each gets half, which saves neither, so both sin. If one yields, he loves the other more than himself and so lacks charity.
claims: Two starving men with one loaf cannot both avoid sin.

rh-l1q2-d1e2650.summary: Fourteenth principal argument: then a sinner could freely and virtuously repent, but virtuous repentance would involve contrary acts at once, sorrow and delight, since virtue acts with pleasure (Ethics III).
claims: Virtuous repentance implies simultaneous sorrow and joy.

rh-l1q2-d1e2691.summary: A reply: this is not absurd for different objects, rejoicing in contrition and grieving for sin.
claims: Joy and sorrow in penance concern different objects.

rh-l1q2-d1e2700.summary: Against: Aristotle says delight excludes contrary sorrow and any sorrow at all. And on Augustine's 'let him always grieve and rejoice in grief', the more one grieves the more one should rejoice, which is impossible.
claims: According to Aristotle, delight excludes sorrow.

rh-l1q2-d1e2723.summary: Further: delight perfects virtuous operation, so would perfect sorrow, but it destroys sorrow.
claims: Delight would both perfect and destroy penitential sorrow.

rh-l1q2-d1e2736.summary: Further: an act of penance is voluntary, and so not penal (Anselm: nothing is penal except against the will), or involuntary, and so not virtuous, or both, which is impossible.
claims: Penance cannot be both penal and voluntary.

rh-l1q2-d1e2749.summary: For the opposite: Aristotle's whole treatment in Ethics III and Metaphysics IX, that rational powers are for opposites while irrational ones are determined to one, and Augustine, Anselm, and Bernard on free choice.
claims: According to Aristotle, rational powers are for opposites.

rh-l1q2-Dd1e2766.summary: Holcot answers that the will is free and lays out nine parts: Anselm on freedom; whether rectitude is distinct from the will; whether the will can be necessitated; whether it is active or passive; whether volition is cognition; whether passions are distinct from operations; whether volition is instantaneous; doubts; and replies.
claims: The created will is free with freedom of contradiction.

rh-l1q2-d1e2771.summary: Holcot answers yes, as everyone must. He will proceed by: Anselm's view of freedom; whether rectitude is distinct from the will; whether a created will can be necessitated; whether the will is active or passive; whether volition is cognition; whether passions of will and intellect are distinct from operations; whether volition is instantaneous or successive; doubts; and replies.
claims: The created will is free with freedom of contradiction in using and enjoying.

rh-l1q2-Dd1e2805.summary: Holcot sets out Anselm's account: 'will' as instrument, affection, and use; the two affections for advantage and justice; rectitude as the affection for justice; and freedom as the power to keep rectitude. He then criticizes it. Augustine's criterion of power is doing what we will, which rectitude fails. The affections are superfluous entities. A distinct rectitude could be removed by God. A single sin cannot destroy an intense habit. Keeping rectitude is due more to grace than to free will. Anselm's proof that God cannot remove rectitude yields only a harmless negative.
claims: Anselm's definition of freedom as power to keep rectitude is inadequate.
Anselm's affections of the will are superfluous entities.

rh-l1q2-d1e2813.summary: Sets out Anselm's view. 'Will' is equivocal: the instrument of willing, its affections, and its use, which requires actual cognition of the object. The instrument is one and constant, its uses many. The will has two affections, for advantage and for justice, which exist without actual cognition, even in a sleeper. The affection for justice is rectitude, separable from the will and varying in degree; the affection for advantage is inseparable and does not vary.
claims: According to Anselm, 'will' signifies instrument, affection, and use.
According to Anselm, the will has affections for advantage and for justice.
According to Anselm, the affection for justice is rectitude.

rh-l1q2-d1e2885.summary: Anselm defines free choice as choice able to keep rectitude, and all freedom as the will's power to keep rectitude, and argues God cannot remove rectitude from the will.
claims: According to Anselm, freedom is the power to keep rectitude.

rh-l1q2-d1e2905.summary: Against the definition: Augustine says nothing is in our power except what happens when we will, and having something in our power converts with being able to do it when we will. We cannot produce rectitude when we will.
claims: According to Augustine, what is in our power is what we do when we will.
Rectitude cannot be produced at will.

rh-l1q2-d1e2937.summary: Further: these affections seem superfluous entities, since everything explained by them is explained by the will alone, and no experience, reason, or scripture requires them, just as sight needs only the visual power and organ, not distinct relations to light, colors, and figures. And if rectitude is a thing distinct from the will, God could separate it, against Anselm.
claims: Anselm's affections are superfluous entities.
If rectitude were a distinct thing, God could remove it.

rh-l1q2-d1e2992.summary: If one says God cannot remove it against the will's wishes: the affection that is the will's work does not prevent God from annihilating it.
claims: Nothing in the will prevents God from annihilating rectitude.

rh-l1q2-d1e3005.summary: Further: Anselm holds the affection is more intense in the just. If someone with very intense rectitude sins mortally, one act cannot destroy the whole habit, since one act cannot corrupt a habit, or we would have privations in our power as we have operations, against Aristotle.
claims: A single act cannot destroy an intense habit.

rh-l1q2-d1e3031.summary: If one says a single mortal act diminishes the whole acquired habit, one must otherwise grant that rectitude could exist in a damned sinner who dies at once.
claims: Rectitude could otherwise remain in the damned.

rh-l1q2-d1e3042.summary: Further: an operation imputed less to free choice than to grace should not define free choice. Anselm himself says keeping rectitude is imputed more to grace, and that free choice has and keeps rectitude only through prevenient and subsequent grace.
claims: According to Anselm, keeping rectitude is due more to grace than to free choice.
Free choice should not be defined by what it does only through another.

rh-l1q2-d1e3086.summary: Further: Anselm's proof that God cannot remove rectitude fails. If God removes it willingly, he does not will the will to will what he wills it to will, but this negative conclusion posits nothing and is not impossible, as a stone or a sleeper of whom God wills nothing satisfies it. 'God wills Socrates to will nothing, so he does not will him to will what he wills him to will' is valid.
claims: Anselm's argument that God cannot remove rectitude yields only a harmless negative.

rh-l1q2-Dd1e3145.summary: After distinctions among freedoms (from necessity, sin, misery), senses of necessity, freedom of indifference versus contradiction, and true versus interpretative freedom, Holcot argues that freedom is the will itself under different connotations, not an added thing. Its nominal definition is the power, given all requisites, to act or not. Rectitude is the will's state of conformity to divine law, sometimes a distinct volition and sometimes the will itself when it conforms by willing nothing.
claims: Freedom is the will itself, connoting different things.
Freedom of contradiction is the power, given all requisites, to act or not.
Freedom of indifference differs from freedom of contradiction.
Rectitude can be the will itself when conforming by willing nothing.

rh-l1q2-d1e3153.summary: States the second article: whether freedom is a thing distinct from the will.

rh-l1q2-d1e3158.summary: Proposes preliminary distinctions to sort out the doctors' different ways of speaking, useful for this and later articles.

rh-l1q2-d1e3169.summary: First distinction, from Lombard (II d. 25): freedom from necessity (i.e. from coercion, held before and after the Fall), from sin (being in grace and able to merit), and from misery (lacking everything harmful and penal).
claims: According to Lombard, there are three freedoms: from necessity, from sin, and from misery.

rh-l1q2-d1e3196.summary: Second distinction: necessity means either coercion or violence, or inevitability, whether violent or not.
claims: Necessity means either coercion or inevitability.

rh-l1q2-d1e3212.summary: Third distinction: freedom from coercion is either freedom of indifference or of contradiction, which are not synonyms. Every freedom of indifference is a freedom of contradiction but not conversely. Indifference means no greater inclination to either side. Contradiction can coexist with an inclination, as one habituated to pray at a set time can pray or not but is more inclined to pray. Strictly, no virtuous or vicious person has freedom of indifference toward virtuous or vicious acts.
claims: Freedom of indifference is distinct from freedom of contradiction.
Freedom of contradiction is compatible with inclination by habit.
The virtuous and vicious lack freedom of indifference.

rh-l1q2-d1e3265.summary: Fourth distinction: something is done freely truly or interpretatively. Truly, when something in one's power precedes it, either deliberation or a previously acquired habit, as Aristotle says we act in sudden matters by habit. Such habitual acts are imputed, praised, or blamed, since their habits are imputable. Interpretatively, when one could deliberate but does not, and assents naturally or by the impetus of custom.
claims: Acts done from acquired habit are truly free and imputable.
Acts done without deliberation one could have made are interpretatively free.

rh-l1q2-d1e3326.summary: Holcot's position: freedom, however taken, stands for the will itself, with different connotations. Freedom from sin connotes being in grace; from misery, being without penalty; from necessity, being uncoercible; of indifference, not being more inclined either way; of contradiction, being able to will either opposite. These terms all stand for one thing but are not synonyms.
claims: Freedom is the will itself, with different connotations.
The various terms for freedom stand for one thing but are not synonyms.

rh-l1q2-d1e3370.summary: Proof that the will is not free by an added thing, as water is hot by added heat: otherwise God could separate it, and the will would no longer be rational, but the will is rational by its essence.
claims: The will is free by its essence, not by an added thing.

rh-l1q2-d1e3388.summary: As to the thing signified, the freedom of the will is the will itself. As to the nominal definition, freedom is a power by which the will, given all causes required for its effect, can co-act with them and produce its act or not as it pleases. This is freedom of contradiction, the subject of the question.
claims: Freedom of contradiction is the will's power, given all requisites, to act or not as it pleases.

rh-l1q2-d1e3413.summary: Is rectitude distinct from the will? The nominal definition of rectitude is not 'willing what God wills it to will', since the will can be right without any willing. It is the will's state of conformity to divine law in willing or not willing as God wills. So rectitude is sometimes a thing distinct from the will, namely a volition conforming to the law, and sometimes the will itself, when it conforms by willing nothing. A will can be as right by not willing as by willing.
claims: Rectitude is the will's conformity to divine law in willing or not willing.
Rectitude is sometimes a volition and sometimes the will itself.
A will can be right by willing nothing.

rh-l1q2-Dd1e3469.summary: Holcot considers whether a created will can be necessitated to act in the manner of nature. He reports a view that it can: by extreme pain or delight, by willing known consequences, and by intense habit, as most human acts proceed from custom rather than deliberation. Supporting arguments come from the practical syllogism and from the finite power of the will. A response locating difficulty only in the passions, whose spirits move slowly, is criticized on the ground that greater temptations are harder to overcome. The article is recited, not asserted.
claims: A created will can be necessitated by extreme pain, delight, or intense habit.
Most human acts are free only interpretatively, from habit.

rh-l1q2-d1e3477.summary: Third article: whether a created will can be necessitated to its act, not by necessity of action but of natural production, i.e. so disposed that it elicits its act in the manner of nature, not freely.

rh-l1q2-d1e3497.summary: One opinion says no: a will testing its freedom can freely love or hate any object, will misery, hate beatitude, and set anything in this life as its end.
claims: According to some, the will can freely love or hate any object.

rh-l1q2-d1e3518.summary: That opinion misses the point. Another opinion says the will can be so disposed, in three or more cases.
claims: The will can be necessitated in certain cases.

rh-l1q2-d1e3530.summary: First case: an intense apprehension of something excessively painful that the will cannot prevent necessitates flight from it.
claims: Intense apprehension of extreme pain necessitates flight.

rh-l1q2-d1e3541.summary: Second case: an intense, unpreventable apprehension of something excessively delightful could necessitate an act of willing or delight in it.
claims: Intense apprehension of extreme delight can necessitate volition.

rh-l1q2-d1e3557.summary: Third case: when the will wills something and knows and wills that something else follows from it, it wills the consequent. Both conditions matter: willing to cross the sea does not imply willing to sail if one does not know sailing is required, and willing to live in a mortal body does not imply willing to die, since the will can be of impossibles (Ethics III), such as flying over the sea or living forever in such a body.
claims: Willing something and willing a known consequent to follow necessitates willing the consequent.
The will can will impossible but imaginable things.

rh-l1q2-d1e3599.summary: Fourth case: a habit can be so intense that, with the other requisites, the will necessarily produces an act like it. Experience shows that human wills mostly act in the manner of nature, free only interpretatively: we deliberate few acts by practical syllogism and are ruled by custom, as in putting on clothing. Aristotle says art does not deliberate, as Averroes illustrates with sewing and weaving.
claims: An intense habit can necessitate acts.
Most human acts proceed from habit in the manner of nature, not deliberation.

rh-l1q2-d1e3660.summary: Introduces arguments for the conclusion that the created will can be necessitated to will and not-will.

rh-l1q2-d1e3669.summary: First argument, from Aristotle on the practical syllogism (Ethics VI): from 'everything sweet should be tasted' and 'this is sweet' the soul at once acts. A practical syllogism necessitates its conclusion as a speculative one does, and an unimpeded agent must act at once.
claims: A practical syllogism necessitates action as a speculative one necessitates assent.

rh-l1q2-d1e3727.summary: Further: the more evident a good, the harder it is to reject. Since the will's power of rejection is finite and a good can appear better and better indefinitely, some good will exceed it and necessitate the will.
claims: A sufficiently apparent good would exceed the will's finite power of rejection.

rh-l1q2-d1e3745.summary: Further: temptation makes difficulty for the will, so there is a maximum difficulty it can overcome or a minimum it cannot, and either way some power exceeds the will.
claims: Some temptation exceeds the will's power.

rh-l1q2-d1e3761.summary: A response: in willing itself there is no difficulty; the difficulty is the sensitive appetite's rebellion. The will cannot at once suppress passions, which remain for a time against its will, because emotions involve local motion of spirits that takes time, as Avicenna, Galen, and the physicians teach. But it can always will them not to be with equal ease. Aristotle likewise says anger cannot be repressed at once.
claims: Willing involves no difficulty; difficulty lies in the sensitive appetite.
Passions involve motion of spirits and so cannot be removed instantly.

rh-l1q2-d1e3838.summary: Against that response: then overcoming greater temptation would be no harder or more praiseworthy for the will than overcoming lesser, since rejecting either is equally easy and suffices, which contradicts experience.
claims: Greater temptations are more praiseworthy to overcome.

rh-l1q2-d1e3862.summary: Further: concupiscence diminishes the gravity of sin and its absence aggravates it, as Augustine says Adam sinned more because desire did not yet resist his will. Desire resists only by making difficulty for the will.
claims: Concupiscence diminishes sin by making difficulty for the will.

rh-l1q2-d1e3888.summary: Further: 'the flesh lusts against the spirit' implies the flesh causes the spirit difficulty.
claims: According to Paul, the flesh makes difficulty for the spirit.

rh-l1q2-d1e3898.summary: Further: then the will could accept any pain of sense without difficulty, the greatest as easily as the least.
claims: The response implies all pains are equally easy to accept.

rh-l1q2-d1e3914.summary: Further: local motion of the body depends partly on the will, and per Anselm the members cannot but obey the will. So if the will could always will against passion, restraining one's hand in great anger would be no harder than when calm, contrary to experience. Willing against passion is therefore harder when passion is present.
claims: The members obey the will in local motion.
Willing against present passion is harder than in its absence.

rh-l1q2-d1e3977.summary: Further: the will rejects temptation only by a contrary volition, and if it suffers no difficulty in that, it suffers none at all, which is false. A note says this article on necessitation is only recited, not asserted.
claims: The will suffers difficulty in rejecting temptation.

rh-l1q2-Dd1e3996.summary: Holcot holds that the will is both active, as a partial efficient cause of its volition, and passive, as its subject. He argues from Aristotle's definition of the voluntary, the freedom a merely passive power would lack, Augustine, and the requirements of merit and sin.
claims: The will is both active and passive regarding its volition.

rh-l1q2-d1e4004.summary: Fourth article: whether the will is an active or passive power.

rh-l1q2-d1e4011.summary: Holcot holds the will is both active, as at least a partial efficient cause of its operation, and passive, as its subject.
claims: The will is both active and passive regarding its operation.

rh-l1q2-d1e4022.summary: Proof: Aristotle defines the voluntary as what has its principle in the agent knowing the particulars, excluding violence and ignorance. The principle must be active, since a passive principle is present even in what suffers violence.
claims: The voluntary requires an active principle in the agent.

rh-l1q2-d1e4063.summary: Further: a passive principle cannot choose to suffer or not when an active object is present, so a merely passive will could not will or not will, and freedom would perish.
claims: A merely passive will would lack freedom.

rh-l1q2-d1e4079.summary: Further: Augustine says an action whose principle is not in the agent is involuntary, so volition without an active principle in man would be involuntary.
claims: According to Augustine, action without an internal principle is involuntary.

rh-l1q2-d1e4090.summary: Further: otherwise merit and demerit would not be in the will's power.
claims: A merely passive will could not merit.

rh-l1q2-d1e4097.summary: Further: a merely receptive will would not sin, since suffering evil or injustice is not sin (Anselm), and Augustine says nothing is so in the will's power as the will itself.
claims: Suffering injustice is not sin.

rh-l1q2-Dd1e4114.summary: Holcot holds that every volition is a complex cognition, an optative mental sentence such as 'would that I had this'. Indicative reports of desire signify acts of will rather than being them.
claims: Every volition is an optative mental sentence.

rh-l1q2-d1e4122.summary: Fifth article: whether volition is cognition.

rh-l1q2-d1e4129.summary: Holcot holds every volition is a complex cognition, though not conversely: every volition or nolition is a mental sentence in the optative mood ('would that I had this') or equivalent. Mental propositions such as 'I desire this' or 'I love this' are not exercised acts of will but signify them. The will can tend only to what appears good to it.
claims: Every volition is a complex cognition.
Volition is an optative mental sentence.
Indicative reports of desire signify but are not acts of will.

rh-l1q2-Dd1e4156.summary: Holcot holds, against many, that delight and passions are things distinct from the operations they follow, following Aristotle's account of delight as a supervening perfection and the new bodily alteration on attaining a desired object. He rejects one weak supporting argument.
claims: Delight is distinct from the operation it perfects.

rh-l1q2-d1e4164.summary: Sixth article: whether delight is distinct from the will, and generally whether passions of will and intellect are things distinct from their operations.

rh-l1q2-d1e4173.summary: Though many deny it, Holcot thinks it better that they are distinct, which fits Aristotle and Averroes. Aristotle says delight perfects operation not as an inherent habit but as a supervening end, as beauty comes to the young. Thomas explains it as a perfection supervening on an already constituted species, so delight is distinct from the operation it follows.
claims: Delight is a thing distinct from the operation it perfects.
According to Aristotle, delight perfects operation as a supervening end.

rh-l1q2-d1e4225.summary: Further: an intense desire for something absent is more pain than pleasure (Averroes). When the desired thing is obtained, delight follows with bodily alteration, which must be due to something new in the will. The volition existed before, so the new thing is delight, distinct from the volition.
claims: A new bodily alteration on attainment requires a new thing in the will, namely delight.

rh-l1q2-d1e4270.summary: Further: delight occurs in the operation of external sense, which involves no act of the appetitive power (Augustine distinguishes seeing from avoiding or seeking), so delight is not appetite. Holcot rejects this argument, since the soul is both appetite and sense, so it would follow that sense is appetite.
claims: The argument from sensory delight fails, since the soul is both sense and appetite.

rh-l1q2-Dd1e4297.summary: Of three views, Holcot tentatively holds that every volition is produced successively in time, with no first instant of willing. Instantaneous volition would allow angels to sin or merit at their first instant, against Augustine and Anselm, would permit unavoidable sin, and would generate paradoxes of instantaneous merit and infinite reward or penalty.
claims: Every volition is produced successively, with no first instant.
Angels could not sin at the instant of creation.

rh-l1q2-d1e4305.summary: Seventh article: whether volition occurs instantaneously or successively.

rh-l1q2-d1e4310.summary: Three views: volition occurs only in time, with no first instant at which 'the will wills' is true; volition can occur instantly; or the thing that is a volition can exist instantly, but there is no first instant at which it is a volition. Unsure between the first two, Holcot holds the first for now: every volition is produced successively in time.
claims: Every volition is produced successively in time.
There is no first instant of willing.

rh-l1q2-d1e4336.summary: The third view is unreasonable. Given the thing first called a volition, there is no reason it is not a volition at first and is later, unless something is connoted that later exists. Fire's heat is not heating at the instant of contact, but is immediately after, since 'heating' connotes heat caused in the wood. Positing such a thing in the will is not evident; it would rather be called an act of the will.
claims: 'Heating' connotes caused heat, so heat is not heating at the instant of contact.
Nothing analogous is evident in the will.

rh-l1q2-d1e4378.summary: Argument that no caused volition can be instantaneous: otherwise an angel could have sinned at the instant of its creation, having knowledge of good and evil and free choice in that instant.
claims: Instantaneous volition would allow sin at the instant of creation.

rh-l1q2-d1e4396.summary: The consequent is false, first by Augustine (City of God XII): vice in a will removes a good that was in it, so the will was good first and the given instant was not the first of its being bad.
claims: According to Augustine, an evil will presupposes a prior good.

rh-l1q2-d1e4412.summary: Second, by Augustine (City of God XI): sin at the first instant would be natural and so not sin, refuting those who read 'the devil sins from the beginning' that way; where there is vice, an unvitiated nature preceded.
claims: According to Augustine, sin at the first instant would be natural and so not sin.

rh-l1q2-d1e4436.summary: Third: if the angel sinned at that instant, it could have avoided the vice, which is impossible at the first instant.
claims: Sin at the first instant would be unavoidable.

rh-l1q2-d1e4443.summary: Fourth: by parity one could merit at the first instant, but then, unable to lose justice before or at that instant, one would keep it necessarily and deserve no more praise for it than for rationality, as Anselm argues.
claims: Merit at the first instant would be necessary and so not praiseworthy.

rh-l1q2-d1e4463.summary: Further: if volition were instantaneous, an angel could sin necessarily. God creates an angel commanding it to love him as soon as possible but suspends its will at the instant of creation. It will love at some instant a, and in the interval it does not love and so sins unavoidably. The command is not unreasonable, since a knowing, free creature that did not love God at once would be ungrateful.
claims: Instantaneous volition allows unavoidable sin in an interval.

rh-l1q2-d1e4505.summary: Further: instantaneous and temporal merit would be equal. If one merits for an instant and another for an hour with equal effort, the latter merits more by a finite proportion, say double. A third meriting for half an hour merits half the second, so as much as the first, which would make continuing merit through time pointless.
claims: Instantaneous merit would equal some temporal merit.

rh-l1q2-d1e4551.summary: Further: one instant of mortal sin would deserve one penalty, and since an angel's nature is finite, there is some penalty a it cannot receive, with a finite ratio to the instant's penalty. In ten instants of any time it could merit a, so it could sin more than God could punish.
claims: Instantaneous sins could accumulate beyond punishable measure.

rh-l1q2-d1e4580.summary: Further: continuing merit or demerit through a time would deserve intensively infinite reward or punishment, since each instant would deserve some reward and there are infinitely many instants.
claims: Merit per instant would yield infinite reward over any time.

rh-l1q2-d1e4613.summary: Against the reply that only the first instant is rewarded: if Socrates and Plato merit alike over an hour except that Plato does not merit at its last instant c, they would be rewarded equally though meriting unequally, or the instant c would earn reward and so would every later instant.
claims: Rewarding only the first instant would equalize unequal merits.

rh-l1q2-d1e4653.summary: Further: one who sinned venially uniformly over a time at whose end he merited would deserve perpetual purgatory or intensively infinite penalty, and mortal sin infinite penalty.
claims: Instantaneous accounting would make venial sins deserve infinite penalty.

rh-l1q2-Dd1e4671.summary: Holcot raises doubts against the seven conclusions and replies to all the principal arguments. Freedom admits degrees only by connotation. One act can love and hate different objects, and one object can be loved and hated under different intentions. Love can exist with nothing loved, with no need for objects in diminished being. The will moves itself as a partial cause with cognition. Free agents have sufficient power when not acting, against Averroes's reading of Physics VIII, whose prime-mover argument rests on the false eternity of motion. Freedom of contradiction is expounded diachronically, as power immediately before the act, with scope distinctions for 'freely'. Self-referential dictates and conditional obligations are resolved by distinguishing conforming from willing conformity, impossible conditions, and the promisor's intention. Free consideration requires prior confused cognition. Doubling one circumstance does not double a sin's gravity, and all mortal sins deserve extensively infinite punishment. Adam could avoid sin when he sinned in the divided sense. Perplexity cases are handled by the logic of obligations and divine dispensation; no one is necessitated to sin, and choosing the lesser evil under necessity is not sin. Further arguments are added that temptation, grace, habit, and complexion can necessitate the will. Penance is a succession of acts of sorrow and joy.
claims: Freedom of contradiction is the will's power immediately before acting to act or not.
Love can exist without an object.
Free agents have sufficient power when not acting.
No one is necessitated to sin; choosing the lesser evil under necessity is not sin.
Insolubilia of obligation are resolved by impossible conditions and intention.
The created will can be necessitated by grace, habit, temptation, or complexion.

rh-l1q2-d1e4676.summary: Eighth article: raises doubts against the seven conclusions: the will is freedom, not an added thing; rectitude is sometimes the will; the will can be necessitated to act in the manner of nature; the will is active and passive; every volition is a complex cognition, an optative sentence; delight is distinct from the volition it follows; volition is successive. Time allows arguing against only some.
claims: The seven conclusions of the preceding articles are summarized.

rh-l1q2-d1e4722.summary: First doubt, against the first conclusion: freedom admits more and less but the will does not, being the soul's substance. The will of the blessed is freer than a wayfarer's, and one unable to sin is freer (Anselm: the power to sin diminishes freedom; Augustine, Enchiridion).
claims: Freedom admits degrees, but the will does not.

rh-l1q2-d1e4759.summary: Second doubt: whether hatred is love. They seem not to be contraries, yet hating Socrates means willing him not to be or to be badly, so his being badly is willed and loved, and the same act is hatred, love, and desire.
claims: Hatred appears to be a kind of love.

rh-l1q2-d1e4786.summary: Third doubt: whether the same thing can be hated and loved at once. It seems not, since that would be willing it well and badly at once.
claims: One cannot will a thing well and badly at once.

rh-l1q2-d1e4802.summary: Against this, a possible case: Socrates hates his father's killer without knowing who it is and loves Plato, who in fact killed his father. So he hates and loves Plato at once.
claims: One can love and hate the same person under different descriptions.

rh-l1q2-d1e4820.summary: Fourth doubt: whether one can love yet love nothing, hate nothing, desire nothing. It seems not: if Socrates loves nothing, there is no love in him.
claims: Loving nothing seems to imply not loving.

rh-l1q2-d1e4836.summary: Further: every act of will has an object, and the object of love is what is loved, so every love has something loved.
claims: Every love has a loved object.

rh-l1q2-d1e4847.summary: Further: Socrates loves, so he wills good to someone, so loves something.
claims: Loving is willing good to someone.

rh-l1q2-d1e4854.summary: Further: Aristotle (De anima III) requires for animal motion an unmoved mover, the appetible, a moved mover, appetite, and the moved animal, so love requires an appetible object moving the will.
claims: According to Aristotle, appetite requires an appetible object.

rh-l1q2-d1e4871.summary: Further: Averroes says what moves appetite is good or apparently good, so every love is of a true or apparent good.
claims: According to Averroes, every love is of a true or apparent good.

rh-l1q2-d1e4884.summary: Further: if love could exist with nothing loved, the highest love could exist with no delight in anything.
claims: Objectless love would permit love without delight.

rh-l1q2-d1e4891.summary: For the opposite, a possible case: Plato loves only Socrates, and Socrates is annihilated while the love remains. Then love is in Plato yet nothing is loved by him, since each singular 'this is not loved' is true.
claims: Love can persist when its object is annihilated, so one can love and love nothing.

rh-l1q2-d1e4909.summary: Further: a sick man desires health yet no health, since he desires neither the health in Socrates nor in Plato nor any other, and every health is one of these.
claims: Desire for health is not desire for any particular health.

rh-l1q2-d1e4932.summary: Further: if Socrates desires to build a castle, there is desire in him but no thing is desired, neither present nor future, since 'Socrates building a castle' is nothing.
claims: Desire for a future state has no existing object.

rh-l1q2-d1e4943.summary: Fifth doubt, against the will's being active: then it would alter itself by successively producing a quality in itself, which is alteration, contrary to Averroes, who denies alteration in the intellective part.
claims: An active will producing its volition successively would alter itself.

rh-l1q2-d1e4975.summary: Similarly Averroes proves that whatever is changed is changed by another.
claims: Whatever is changed is changed by another.
concepts: omne quod movetur ab alio movetur

rh-l1q2-d1e4982.summary: Further: the will would be in act and potency to the same thing, as agent and recipient, which Averroes treats as impossible.
claims: Nothing is both agent and patient of the same effect.

rh-l1q2-d1e5002.summary: Further: the will is not the efficient cause of its delight, which follows apprehension like a shadow (Averroes), so it is not the cause of its act.
claims: Delight follows apprehension, not the will.

rh-l1q2-d1e5022.summary: Confirmation: apprehension is caused from outside and delight necessarily follows it, so delight is caused from outside.
claims: Delight is caused from outside.

rh-l1q2-d1e5031.summary: Further: if the will caused its delight, it would cause its sorrow, and the damned could make their penalty not afflictive.
claims: If the will caused its sorrow, the damned could avoid suffering.

rh-l1q2-d1e5040.summary: Further: as volition is to sorrow, so to delight. Sorrow is caused wholly from outside and volition follows it necessarily, so delight too, and volition follows delight naturally.
claims: Volition follows sorrow and delight naturally.

rh-l1q2-d1e5063.summary: Further: if the will were a sufficient efficient cause of volition, given cognition of a delightful object it could will or not will. But at the instant it begins to will, either it now first has sufficient power, so some change occurred, whose source is external (so the act is not free) or internal (and then if it could cause that change earlier it would have done so), or it had sufficient power earlier and so would have willed earlier.
claims: A will's beginning to act requires a prior change in it or outside it.

rh-l1q2-d1e5133.summary: If it now first can cause that change, some prior change made it able, and so on to infinity, with every change preceded by another.
claims: Self-initiated volition leads to an infinite regress of changes.

rh-l1q2-d1e5159.summary: Further: with sufficient cognition and no volition, the will cannot begin willing unless moved from outside, since otherwise it would be uniform in all its dispositions whether it causes volition or not.
claims: A uniformly disposed will cannot begin willing without external motion.

rh-l1q2-d1e5181.summary: Confirmation from Averroes (Physics VIII): a mover moves only when it has the disposition to move; a power for contraries with the same proportion does neither; no rational power acts after not acting without prior change in itself or outside. Since cognition was already present, something else external is required, so the will is only passive.
claims: According to Averroes, no rational power begins to act without prior change.

rh-l1q2-d1e5230.summary: Further: an active power is a principle of change in another as other (Metaphysics IX), so an active will's volition would not be immanent.
claims: Active power acts on another, so volition would not be immanent.

rh-l1q2-d1e5243.summary: Further: Aristotle (De anima III) calls the will a moved mover and the appetible an unmoved mover, so the will is moved by the object and is merely passive in willing.
claims: According to Aristotle, the will is moved by the appetible.

rh-l1q2-d1e5260.summary: Reply to the first doubt: freedom is the will.
claims: Freedom is the will.

rh-l1q2-d1e5265.summary: Denies the inference. It follows only that 'freedom' is not synonymous with 'will', since it connotes something other than what it principally signifies, and so can be predicated of different wills in greater or lesser degree.
claims: 'Freedom' admits degrees because of what it connotes, not what it signifies.

rh-l1q2-d1e5283.summary: Reply to the second doubt: the same act can be hatred and love with respect to different objects, as one volition 'may Socrates be killed so that Plato is promoted' wills end and means. One act is willing Socrates not to be, hating him, and desiring that state. Love and hatred are contraries only toward the same object, as double and half are opposed only relative to the same thing.
claims: One act can be love and hatred toward different objects.
Love and hatred are contrary only with respect to the same object.

rh-l1q2-d1e5316.summary: Reply to the third doubt: the same thing can be hated and loved at once when apprehended through two propositions or intentions, each a partial cause of one act, as in the case of the unknown killer who is Plato.
claims: The same thing can be loved and hated at once under different intentions.

rh-l1q2-d1e5342.summary: Reply to the fourth doubt, which leads some to posit things in cognized, diminished being: 'Socrates loves' and 'Socrates loves nothing' are compatible. 'Socrates loves' signifies only that love is in Socrates. By that love something is sometimes loved, when its object exists, and sometimes nothing, when it does not.
claims: One can love and yet love nothing.
'Socrates loves' signifies only that love inheres in him.
Positing objects in diminished being is unnecessary.

rh-l1q2-d1e5364.summary: Denies 'Socrates loves nothing, so there is no love in Socrates'.
claims: Loving nothing does not imply lacking love.

rh-l1q2-d1e5372.summary: Denies that every love has a loved object.
claims: Not every love has a loved object.

rh-l1q2-d1e5379.summary: Denies 'Plato loves, so he wills good to someone'; perhaps he only thinks he does.
claims: Loving does not imply willing good to an existing someone.

rh-l1q2-d1e5386.summary: Reply to Aristotle's appetible mover. Averroes's example of the bath: it has a form in the soul by which it causes desire and a form outside as end. The bath is not literally in the soul; its intention, species, or cognition is, as a partial cause of desire. The appetible required may be only in the soul, as an animal may flee as truly with no fearsome thing outside as if one appeared.
claims: The appetible that moves appetite may be only a cognition in the soul.
Cognition of an object is a partial cause of desire.

rh-l1q2-d1e5436.summary: Reply to the fifth: grants that there can be love without a thing it concerns, which is not doubtful.
claims: Love can exist without an object.

rh-l1q2-d1e5447.summary: Reply to the fifth doubt: the will is both active and passive toward its act as a partial cause. The preceding cognition is also a cause of volition, and whatever causes that cognition is in some way a cause of the volition.
claims: The will is a partial cause of its act, with cognition as a co-cause.

rh-l1q2-d1e5464.summary: Reply to the argument from Physics VII. Though Aristotle there denies alteration in the intellective part, in De anima II he says the learner is altered in passing to a habit and the knower is changed in some way in passing to act, and Averroes repeatedly says the intellect is altered. Aristotle's aim in Physics VII is to prove there is no infinite regress in movers and moved.
claims: According to De anima II, the intellect is altered in learning.
Physics VII aims to exclude infinite regress in movers.

rh-l1q2-d1e5528.summary: Aristotle first proves that in such motion some mover is moved, inductively for local motion, then for alteration, which concerns sensible qualities of the third species where mover and moved are together. Qualities in the intellective part come from the senses, so mover and moved are always together, as phantasm or agent intellect with possible intellect.
claims: In every motion the mover is together with the moved.

rh-l1q2-d1e5563.summary: If Aristotle's main aim is that mover and moved are together, denying alteration in the intellect does not falsify that. In that passage he seems to follow Plato's view of knowledge as concreated with the soul, on which learning involves no alteration; on Aristotle's own view the soul is altered with alterer and altered together.
claims: Aristotle's denial of intellectual alteration reflects Plato's view.
On Aristotle's own view the soul is altered in learning.

rh-l1q2-d1e5602.summary: Reply to 'whatever is moved is moved by another': the will is moved by itself as partial cause and by another, since it never causes volition without prior cognition of what is willed, and so is not moved by itself as total cause.
claims: The will moves itself only as a partial cause.

rh-l1q2-d1e5618.summary: Reply to the act-and-potency argument: it would be absurd for something to have a thing and be in potency to it, but the will is not actually willing before it wills, only in potency, able to bring itself to act together with cognition.
claims: The will is in potency before willing and actualizes itself with cognition.

rh-l1q2-d1e5638.summary: Reply to the argument from delight. Even if delight followed cognition naturally (as some say of the clear vision of God) and volition followed delight, it would not follow that volition is wholly external; it would be from the will naturally, not freely. Not being free does not mean not being effected by the will. The will can cause its delight indirectly, by continuing attention to a delightful object and joining sense cognition to it, and likewise intensify sorrow by dwelling on its causes.
claims: A volition can be from the will naturally rather than freely.
The will can indirectly cause delight or sorrow by directing attention.

rh-l1q2-d1e5713.summary: Reply to the argument that the will must differ in disposition when it causes volition. The Physics VIII principle concerns external local motion, and taken literally it is false of free agents and of God. A free agent has sufficient power to will when not willing, which is why it is free. When it causes volition it is informed by it but receives nothing new by which it co-acts. There is no first instant of willing, and from having sufficient power earlier it does not follow that it willed earlier, as it would for a natural agent.
claims: A free agent has sufficient power to act when not acting.
The will receives nothing new that enables its volition.
The Physics VIII principle is false of free agents and God.

rh-l1q2-d1e5801.summary: Reply to the fourth: the same answer. Averroes's principle that a mover moves only when newly disposed is false, as God has sufficient power to make other worlds and does not, and had it before creating this one. Aristotle's arguments in Physics VIII for a separated unmoved prime mover rest on false premises, the eternity of motion and time, so the whole book is too weak and its authority need not be accepted.
claims: God has power to create other worlds and does not exercise it.
Aristotle's Physics VIII argument for the prime mover rests on the false eternity of motion.

rh-l1q2-d1e5849.summary: Reply to the definition of active power: Aristotle's definition, 'principle of change in another or as other', implies something can change itself as lacking a perfection it can give itself, and so the will changes itself to volition, speaking broadly.
claims: Active power can change itself as other.

rh-l1q2-d1e5880.summary: Reply to De anima III. Aristotle speaks for teaching purposes about the common case of animals moved by a sensed appetible, which moves by causing its cognition and appetite. He does not deny that perfect animals desire what they do not see, even nothing, as desiring roses in winter. 'Appetible' covers both the real object and its intention, a partial cause, so the appetitive power is only a partial efficient cause of its act.
claims: One can desire what does not exist, such as roses in winter.
The appetitive power is a partial efficient cause of its act.

rh-l1q2-d1e5926.summary: Reply to the first principal argument. Grants that the will can freely will and freely not will. A possibility proposition is not 'posited in being' by asserting the will wills and does not will at a, but by 'it wills at a and immediately before could have not willed at a'. Also 'this is possible: the will freely wills' does not imply that this proposition can be true, just as 'it is possible that no proposition is true' and 'God can create nothing' are possible yet can never be true: they are possible because things can be as they signify.
claims: Freedom of contradiction concerns the power immediately before the act.
A possible proposition need not be able to be true.

rh-l1q2-d1e5999.summary: Alternatively, 'the will can freely will' is ambiguous: 'freely' can modify the first verb (true) or the second (false). Granting 'the will freely wills' and 'freely does not will' as possible, they mean that, given all requisites, the will has in its power to begin or not begin to will, and wills freely because it can stop when it likes. It is not called free by a freedom of contradiction toward the act it now has, but by its freedom to continue or discontinue willing in the future.
claims: The will is free by its power to begin, continue, or stop willing, not toward its present act.

rh-l1q2-d1e6050.summary: Objection: if the will wills, it necessarily will will for some time, so cannot freely not will in the future. Granted: if it wills, it necessarily will will for some time, but for no particular time necessarily. Since it can sometimes will for this or that future time, an hour or half, it is called free from that power over the future, though not in acts where it is necessitated to act in the manner of nature.
claims: A willing will must will for some time but for no particular time.
Freedom concerns power over the future duration of willing.

rh-l1q2-d1e6083.summary: Note repeating the analysis: 'the will can indifferently will and not will at a' is expounded as 'it wills at a and immediately before could have not willed at a' or the converse. Many propositions are possible though their being true is impossible, since possibility means things can be as they signify.
claims: Possibility propositions are expounded diachronically.

rh-l1q2-d1e6133.summary: Repeats the alternative: 'the will can freely will' depends on whether 'freely' determines the preceding or subsequent verb, true in the first case and false in the second.
claims: The scope of 'freely' determines the truth of 'the will can freely will'.

rh-l1q2-d1e6146.summary: Reply to the second argument: 'a man freely understands' is granted in the same way, not as being in potency of contradiction at the instant, but as having had, immediately before beginning, the power to begin or not.
claims: Understanding can be free in the diachronic sense.

rh-l1q2-d1e6166.summary: Reply to the third argument: denies that the will could choose which of many similar volitions to cause, since it is only a partial cause of willing, and so it causes this volition first, not another.
claims: As a partial cause, the will does not choose among indiscernible volitions.

rh-l1q2-d1e6184.summary: Objection: the causes, will and cognition, are the same throughout an hour of continuous cognition in which one loves with a, stops, loves with b exactly like a, stops. Why does the will produce a rather than b in the first part? If time or the heavens is somehow a cause, it is easy to solve.
claims: Identical causes producing distinct similar acts raise a problem of individuation.

rh-l1q2-d1e6207.summary: Reply to the fourth argument: an act that is not is not in the will's power, since every act is. 'Before the will has its act, its act is in its power' is literally false and improper, but is admitted in usage for 'the will can freely cause its act'. When the will wills, 'this act is in the will's power' may be granted, since it can continue the act longer or shorter.
claims: 'The act is in the will's power' before it exists is improper speech.
An existing act is in the will's power as to its continuation.

rh-l1q2-d1e6238.summary: Reply to the fifth: denies that freely not willing is willing. 'Freely does not will' is said from the preceding power by which, when it began not to will, it could have willed. So the will freely does not will by willing nothing. Freedom is used positively or negatively, and negatively by willing nothing.
claims: The will can freely not will by willing nothing.
Freedom can be exercised negatively.

rh-l1q2-d1e6265.summary: Reply to the second principal argument. If 'suspend its act' means freely having no act, the will can suspend every act by freely willing nothing. If it means willing to have no act, then 'the will freely suspends every act' is contradictory, as the argument concludes.
claims: The will can suspend all acts by freely willing nothing.
Willing to have no act is contradictory.

rh-l1q2-d1e6313.summary: Reply to the third principal argument: denies both the inference and the consequent. As the arguments show, cognition can be sustained by an excellent sensible or intelligible so that the will cannot destroy it, as near a fire, and in separated intellects. Damned souls and those in purgatory have intellections they cannot cut off. Even if the will is queen, it cannot do whatever it wills, being so wondrous that it sometimes wills impossibles; intellect and sense cannot obey all its commands.
claims: The will cannot cut off every cognition.
Damned and purgatorial souls cannot stop their intellections.
The will can will impossibles.

rh-l1q2-d1e6359.summary: Reply to Anselm: he means only that no act of sensing is sin unless commanded by the will. Calling the will queen and the intellect reason is also inexact, since intellect and will are the same thing, so the intellect would be ruler of itself.
claims: Acts of sense are sinful only when commanded by the will.
Intellect and will are the same thing.

rh-l1q2-d1e6392.summary: Reply to the argument from recollection. For Aristotle, recollecting is recalling what one has forgotten, which one can never do at will, so recollection depends on a bodily organ. Conversely, if understanding is immaterial, the will has power over some intelligible, but not all.
claims: Recollection is never at will and depends on a bodily organ.
The will has power over some but not all intellection.

rh-l1q2-d1e6419.summary: Reply to the argument from rational powers: a rational power sometimes operates in the manner of nature, not freely, and then no joining will is required.
claims: Rational powers sometimes act naturally without the will.

rh-l1q2-d1e6430.summary: Reply to Augustine's joining will, deferring the full difficulty.
