In some intellections the will concurs, as when one has a species, understands by it, delights, and strives to continue, so the will metaphorically joins parent and offspring. Likewise in sense a species can be received without seeing when one is intensely occupied elsewhere, because, per Augustine, no will joins the species, i.e. there is no attention, which is the vision. Augustine's sayings here are metaphorical adaptations with a slight likeness to his point.
claims: The will concurs in some intellections by sustaining attention.
A sense species can be present without perception when attention is absent.
Augustine's trinitarian language about cognition is metaphorical.

rh-l1q2-d1e6500.summary: Reply to the fourth principal argument: denies the inference for both parts, since the will cannot conform to every judgment. It is possible for the will to will against every judgment, as when Socrates has only the judgment 'go to church at a' and wills against it. But there is a judgment the will cannot will against, 'one should not live miserably', since Holcot holds it impossible to will to be miserable, though one can will not to be blessed or not to be, as the next question will say.
claims: The will cannot will to be miserable.
The will can will not to be blessed or not to be.

rh-l1q2-d1e6547.summary: The will's conforming to a judgment differs from its willing conformity. If reason dictates willing nothing during hour a and Socrates sleeps through it, his will conforms without willing conformably. Conforming is making things as the judgment principally signifies; willing conformably is wishing them so. Some judgments, like 'never will', cannot be willed conformably.
claims: Conforming to a judgment differs from willing conformably to it.
Some judgments cannot be willed conformably.

rh-l1q2-d1e6595.summary: Reply to the self-referential judgment a, 'one should will against every judgment'. Socrates can will against a and will to diverge from it, since he can have an opposed judgment, and willing to conform to that is willing to diverge from a.
claims: One can will against a self-referential dictate by holding an opposed judgment.

rh-l1q2-d1e6621.summary: Grants that if he wills against that judgment, he does not will against every judgment.
claims: Willing against the dictate is not willing against every judgment.

rh-l1q2-d1e6633.summary: Denies that it follows he does not will against a. With that judgment alone, the will cannot freely will in conformity or nonconformity to it, since either leads to the other; the judgment passes without any volition following, so the will does not will conformably. Alternatively, it can will against the judgment but never conform to it wholly, since the judgment signifies both that one should and should not will against it.
claims: With only a self-referential dictate, no volition can conform or diverge consistently.
Such a dictate passes without volition.

rh-l1q2-d1e6711.summary: Reply to the second form: grants that the will cannot conform to every judgment, though the argument fails. The will conforms to 'will nothing before tomorrow' by not willing, but such conformity is neither praiseworthy nor virtuous, since it was never willed. It cannot will to conform to that dictate before tomorrow.
claims: Conformity by not willing is not praiseworthy if not willed.

rh-l1q2-d1e6744.summary: Reply to the third form: grants the conclusion. Such a dictate would be erroneous, since one should will neither a neighbor's damnation nor one's own mortal sin. By law, though, one should will against a neighbor's damnation less than against one's own mortal sin.
claims: One should will neither one's neighbor's damnation nor one's own sin.
One should oppose one's own sin more than a neighbor's damnation.

rh-l1q2-d1e6775.summary: Alternatively, the key premise 'Socrates wills Plato damned more than to sin mortally' is false, since 'than' distributes its term confusedly and distributively over every mortal sin Socrates can commit. One may descend to the sin 'Socrates wills Plato damned', yielding the contradiction, as 'a pearl is whiter than a man' implies whiter than Socrates, Plato, Peter.
claims: 'Than' distributes its term confusedly and distributively.
The premise is false because it implies preferring a thing to itself.

rh-l1q2-d1e6830.summary: Reply to the fourth form: grants that one can sin mortally without any act of will. In a sin of omission no interior or exterior act corresponds; one sins mortally by lacking an act one is bound to by divine precept and freely does not will to have.
claims: One can sin mortally without any act of will, by omission.

rh-l1q2-d1e6859.summary: Reply to the fifth form: given a clearest judgment, the will can still not will it, though it cannot will the opposite while the judgment stands, so it can suspend its act. Alternatively, a clear judgment of one opposite sufficiently represents both, as 'one should go to church with right intention' gives the will enough knowledge to elicit either.
claims: A clear judgment allows suspension but not willing the opposite.
A clear judgment of one opposite represents both to the will.

rh-l1q2-d1e6904.summary: Reply to the sixth form: 'Socrates wills what is most to God's honor more than anything for his own advantage' is false, since 'than' distributes over 'pertaining to his advantage', which includes willing what is most to God's honor, yielding willing it more than itself.
claims: Comparative preference statements can be false through distribution over the compared term.

rh-l1q2-d1e6928.summary: Reply to the fifth principal argument. Some say that in such cases one who binds himself conditionally is bound whether or not the condition is fulfilled, and so deny 'he gave under this condition, it is not fulfilled, so he is not bound'.
claims: According to some, paradoxical conditional obligations bind regardless of the condition.

rh-l1q2-d1e6950.summary: In the case the opposite follows: when one binds oneself conditionally and from the opposite of the condition it follows that one is bound, one is bound by that obligation. If the case is posed as 'Socrates owes Plato ten if Plato meets at a a man who does not owe him, and not otherwise', and Plato meets Socrates, the case is impossible, since its first part makes the two convertible and its second part denies it.
claims: The self-referential conditional obligation, so posed, is an impossible case.

rh-l1q2-d1e6987.summary: If one supposes only that Socrates owes under the condition, the case is possible, and he is bound whether or not the condition holds: if it does not, Plato meets a man who owes him. The inference 'the condition is not fulfilled, so he is not bound' fails.
claims: Under the possible version of the case, Socrates is bound either way.

rh-l1q2-d1e7013.summary: Reply to the manumission case: Plato is free and Socrates a slave, since Plato's freedom follows from both fulfillment and non-fulfillment of the condition, while Socrates' follows only from a fulfillment that cannot occur. 'Plato is free, so he meets a free man' is denied.
claims: In the manumission case Plato is free and Socrates is not.

rh-l1q2-d1e7034.summary: Reply to the Peter and John case: the case is admitted, and neither side follows, since 'Peter wills to enter if John does' is willing only under condition, the act bearing on the whole conditional, so 'Peter wills to enter if John does, so Peter wills to enter' fails. Objection: the earlier reply assumed that one binding oneself conditionally is bound even when the condition fails.
claims: A conditional volition is not a volition of its consequent.

rh-l1q2-d1e7074.summary: Against that assumption: the form of obligation is the whole reason one is bound, and it binds only on fulfillment of the condition, so failure of the condition cannot make one bound.
claims: One is bound only according to the form of the obligation.

rh-l1q2-d1e7094.summary: Further: if something implies an effect as its precise cause, its opposite does not imply the same effect, and fulfillment of the condition is the precise cause of the obligation.
claims: The opposite of a precise cause does not imply the same effect.

rh-l1q2-d1e7116.summary: Further: at instant a, when Socrates would be bound, Plato meets a man bound to him and no other, so the condition fails and Socrates is not bound. So it is more reasonable to say that in this case Socrates is not bound.
claims: In the self-referential case Socrates is not bound.

rh-l1q2-d1e7134.summary: Explanation: whoever binds himself under an impossible condition is bound to nothing, and a condition that becomes impossible through a later event, not voluntarily caused by the promisor, also binds to nothing. Here the condition cannot be wholly fulfilled at a, since supposing it is entails a contradiction. Against the opponent's principle Holcot sets an equally reasonable one: when at the time of fulfillment the condition itself implies that the promisor is not bound, he is not bound. Here both the condition and its opposite imply this. And the opponent himself admits the case is impossible as posed.
claims: A condition impossible at the time of fulfillment binds to nothing.
If both the condition and its opposite imply non-obligation, the promisor is not bound.

rh-l1q2-d1e7256.summary: Further: a condition repugnant to the principal contract voids it, as a marriage 'on condition that I never render the debt' is null. Here fulfillment of the condition implies Socrates is not bound, which is repugnant to the contract, so it is void.
claims: A condition repugnant to the principal contract voids it.

rh-l1q2-d1e7299.summary: Reply to the counterargument: grants 'if Socrates is not bound, Plato meets at a a man not bound to him', but denies 'so he fulfills the condition', since fulfilling a condition is making things wholly as it signifies. At a the condition converts with an impossible copulative, so it is not fulfilled. The promisor's intention was that fulfillment imply obligation, whereas what occurs implies non-obligation.
claims: Fulfilling a condition is making things wholly as it signifies according to the promisor's intention.

rh-l1q2-d1e7350.summary: Reply to the sixth principal argument: the parts of the love case are incompossible, since the first two yield 'Socrates loves everyone who loves him and loves Plato' while the third yields its contradictory.
claims: The case of circular love is incompossible.

rh-l1q2-d1e7374.summary: Reply to the similarity case: denies 'Socrates wills to be like Plato and Plato like Socrates, so they will to be alike', since the consequent signifies willing a quality of the same species, which the antecedent does not; the antecedent has two causes of truth, the consequent one, so there is a fallacy of the consequent.
claims: The similarity argument commits a fallacy of the consequent.

rh-l1q2-d1e7405.summary: Reply to the seventh principal argument. Aristotle and Averroes mean that one with a habit of science can use it without external sense action, through what is in memory together with the will, not that the will alone suffices. Whoever passes freely from habitual to actual consideration first has a confused cognition of the object and knows what considering is, and by that can will to consider it distinctly. One cannot pass by will from habitual to distinct cognition without first reaching confused cognition.
claims: Free consideration requires prior confused cognition of the object.
The will alone does not suffice to actualize a habit.

rh-l1q2-d1e7460.summary: Reply to the first form: it concludes only that before considering a distinctly one considers it confusedly. Confused consideration suffices for willing to know a, though not for willing a distinctly; willing a distinctly requires distinct cognition, willing to know a distinctly only confused cognition.
claims: Confused cognition suffices to will to know something distinctly.

rh-l1q2-d1e7482.summary: Reply on recollection: one can recall freely because one has in oneself the principle of the act, not by volition alone. Whoever wills to recall already recalls, perhaps confusedly, and by that seeks distinct recall. Augustine says the love of one wanting to know what he does not know is love of what he knows.
claims: Willing to recall presupposes confused recall.
According to Augustine, the desire to know is love of what is already known.

rh-l1q2-d1e7513.summary: Reply to the third: all comes to the same, since by confused cognition of a one deliberates whether to consider a distinctly or longer. Objection: 'I will to know what I do not know, so I will what I do not know'.
claims: Deliberation about considering uses confused cognition.

rh-l1q2-d1e7527.summary: Further objection: 'I would know what I in no way know, so I will what I in no way cognize'.
claims: Willing to know the wholly unknown seems to will the unknown.

rh-l1q2-d1e7534.summary: Reply with Augustine (De trinitate XI): I will to know what I do not know in particular, but it does not follow that I will what I do not know, since I know what it is to know what I do not know, which suffices for willing.
claims: Knowing what it is to know suffices for willing to know the unknown.

rh-l1q2-d1e7552.summary: Reply to the second: willing what I know in no way, neither generally nor specially, is impossible, since through general intentions such as 'knowable' I have confused cognition of every knowable.
claims: General intentions give confused cognition of every knowable.

rh-l1q2-d1e7572.summary: Reply to the fourth: grants that the will can divert the intellect from a to b, but only if the intellect apprehends a determinately and b confusedly; then it can will to know b more distinctly. The will can in no way divert the intellect to the wholly unknown.
claims: The will can redirect attention only to what is at least confusedly known.

rh-l1q2-d1e7598.summary: Reply to the eighth principal argument: it rests entirely on Anselm's authority (De casu diaboli 12), and one burdened by it can easily unburden himself by denying that authority.
claims: The argument rests solely on Anselm's authority, which may be denied.

rh-l1q2-d1e7611.summary: Reply to the ninth principal argument: grants the inference. To the alternating case, one may say he should be damned, since at a it is true that immediately before a he was bad, which suffices for being finally bad. Objection: immediately before a he was also good, since no time preceded after which he was good.
claims: Being bad immediately before death suffices for final badness.

rh-l1q2-d1e7638.summary: Further objection: after each sin he repented, so was finally good. Admitting the case one must grant both. So the case may be denied: probably there is a minimal time in which a creature can merit, or a maximal time in which it cannot. Alternation must stop at that limit, and he is judged by the state he is in at death, which is more plausible.
claims: There is probably a minimal time for meriting.
One is judged by one's state at the instant of death.

rh-l1q2-d1e7673.summary: Reply to the second form: denies that God cannot judge because there is no maximal degree; he judges by the degree the soul has at the first instant of its non-being, the instant of death.
claims: God judges by the degree of merit at the instant of death.

rh-l1q2-d1e7697.summary: Reply to the third: Socrates and Plato are rewarded equally, since they merited equally. No merit corresponds to an instant distinct from that of the time, so the soul is rewarded by its degree at death. Being longer in grace without meritorious operation does not increase reward, since we merit by acts, not habits or powers (Ethics I).
claims: No merit corresponds to an instant distinct from the merit of the time.
Being in grace without meritorious acts does not increase reward.
We merit by acts, not by habits or powers.

rh-l1q2-d1e7743.summary: Reply to the fourth: denies antecedent, inference, and consequent, taking a sin of infinite malice as one deserving intensively infinite punishment. He also denies that Socrates sins twice as gravely as Plato.
claims: Socrates does not sin twice as gravely by lacking a good end.

rh-l1q2-d1e7765.summary: Explanation: when many factors concur in an effect, as ten men pull a ship, doubling all doubles the effect, but doubling one factor does not. Many circumstances concur in the gravity of parricide: the law's prohibition, plotting against one's blood, intention, the father's usefulness to the republic, time, place. Doubling one circumstance, such as a half-as-good end, makes the sin graver but not in any definite proportion. A mortal sin is infinitely graver than a venial one without being of infinite malice in the sense of deserving intensively infinite punishment.
claims: Doubling one circumstance does not double the gravity of a sin.
Gravity of sin results from many concurrent circumstances.
Mortal sin is infinitely graver than venial without being of infinite malice.

rh-l1q2-d1e7857.summary: Reply to the fifth: willing to kill two is not twice as grave, since doubling one circumstance does not double the whole sin's gravity, though it increases it in some particular proportion.
claims: Willing to kill two is not twice as grave as willing to kill one.

rh-l1q2-d1e7871.summary: Reply to the sixth likewise: willing to sin for two days is not twice as grave as for one.
claims: Willing to sin for two days is not twice as grave.

rh-l1q2-d1e7878.summary: Reply to the seventh: willing to sin forever is not infinitely graver than for a day, since no mortal sin is infinitely graver than another as measured by punishment. Every mortal sin deserves extensively infinite punishment, and no punishment is double an extensively infinite one. The 'other things being equal' assumption is impossible here.
claims: No mortal sin is infinitely graver than another in punishment.
Every mortal sin deserves extensively infinite punishment.

rh-l1q2-d1e7922.summary: Reply to the drunkenness argument. Someone answers insufficiently with a parallel: by the same reasoning, one in other mortal sins who loves sobriety would deserve infinite reward for the infinite goods it could bring, which is false, since he is not rewarded at all if he dies in mortal sin. Holcot: if 'infinite' is intensive, the claim is false; if extensive, true, since the punishment is infinite in duration.
claims: Drunkenness is infinitely grave only extensively, by the duration of punishment.
Potential consequences do not make a sin intensively infinite.

rh-l1q2-d1e7994.summary: Reply to the perjury case: someone says that in that case Socrates cannot sin two mortal sins, drunkenness and perjury, without sinning infinitely many, but denies that the punishment is intensively infinite, since all may be punished by one extensively infinite penalty, or God does not inflict distinct penalties.
claims: Infinitely many sins may be punished by one extensively infinite penalty.

rh-l1q2-d1e8018.summary: Reply to the tenth principal argument: denies the inference, since the will can will impossibles (Ethics III). The will can will, but not instantaneously, only successively, as article seven said.
claims: The will can will only successively, not instantly.

rh-l1q2-d1e8034.summary: Reply to the seventeen sub-arguments of the tenth. To the first: lack of resistance does not imply instantaneous action, as Averroes implies; the heavenly movers meet no resistance yet move in time, and an angel moves locally in time. Volition has intensive parts that allow a true resistance to its production.
claims: Absence of resistance does not imply instantaneous action.
Volition has intensive parts that ground resistance.

rh-l1q2-d1e8064.summary: Reply to the second: grants that what is moved will necessarily be moved for some time after, but for no particular time, as one who sins will sin afterward but for no time necessarily.
claims: What moves must continue for some time but for no particular time.

rh-l1q2-d1e8080.summary: Reply to the third: grants that Christ did not merit at the first instant of conception, but began to merit, so merited from (not at) the first instant (Lombard III d. 18).
claims: Christ merited from, not at, the first instant of conception.

rh-l1q2-d1e8099.summary: Reply to the fourth: Christ is on the altar suddenly in a sacramental way, by a volition successively produced and conserved through time, not an instantaneous one. Before he was there he willed to be there for some time, as I now will to be in Rome for some time. But perhaps the deity so co-acts that Christ's volition is produced instantly or in time as God pleases.
claims: Christ is sacramentally present suddenly by a successively produced volition.
Christ's volition may be produced instantly by divine co-action.

rh-l1q2-d1e8134.summary: Reply to the fifth, on illumination: the will does not act instantly except when its action terminates a successive change (Averroes, Physics VI). Free volition can follow action only in time, so cannot be instantaneous.
claims: Free volition cannot be instantaneous.

rh-l1q2-d1e8152.summary: Reply to the sixth: denies that the intellect understands instantly. Intellection, vision, and delight are acquired by parts in their generation but can then remain in quiet being, perfect at an instant, unlike alteration, which is always in time. So they are not essentially alterations, and Aristotle proves delight is not generation or alteration since it is perfect at an instant.
claims: Intellection and volition are acquired successively but rest perfect at an instant.
Intellection, vision, and delight are not essentially alterations.

rh-l1q2-d1e8200.summary: Reply to the seventh: denies the inference about delight following apprehension, as a fallacy of the consequent.
claims: The inference from delight's following apprehension commits a fallacy of the consequent.

rh-l1q2-d1e8208.summary: Replies to the eighth and ninth: denies both antecedent and inference, as in the fifth; natural agents do not act instantly except as noted.
claims: Vision and natural agency are not instantaneous in the relevant sense.

rh-l1q2-d1e8219.summary: Reply to the tenth: at the instant the devil began to sin, both 'immediately after this he will sin' and 'immediately after this he is obdurate' would have been true if formed.
claims: At the devil's first instant of sin, sin and obduracy both follow immediately.

rh-l1q2-d1e8237.summary: A difficulty: at that instant it seems true that 'he is in grace and never will be again', since there is either a first instant of non-grace (and so of non-sin) or a last instant of grace, a permanent thing. Reply: where God is the agent, things are not as in natural changes, of which Aristotle says there is no last instant of a permanent thing's being, so this is not absurd.
claims: Divine action can have a last instant of a permanent thing's being, unlike natural change.

rh-l1q2-d1e8274.summary: Reply to the eleventh: grants there is neither a first nor a last instant of volition. But there is no interval between sin and punishment, since just as there is no first instant of sin there is none of punishment: in sinning one deprives oneself of grace and continuously punishes oneself, as Augustine means by 'he repays by suffering what he would not by doing'.
claims: There is no first or last instant of volition.
Sin is its own continuous punishment by loss of grace.

rh-l1q2-d1e8300.summary: Reply to the twelfth: grants that sin did not precede punishment in time, as Augustine says, but by causality or nature: 'he is punished because he sinned' and 'had he not sinned he would not be punished' are true. Averroes speaks of agents by change and completed effects.
claims: Sin precedes punishment by causality, not duration.

rh-l1q2-d1e8329.summary: Reply to the thirteenth: grants for now there is a last instant of charity, since charity is neither caused nor destroyed by a creature but ceases when God stops conserving it, and he can begin not to conserve it at an instant.
claims: There is a last instant of charity, since God ceases to conserve it.

rh-l1q2-d1e8346.summary: Reply to the fourteenth: grants that someone sinned yet never sinned in any time that was the precise measure of his sin of omission, if there is no minimal time for willing or maximal time for not willing.
claims: A sin of omission may have no time that precisely measures it.

rh-l1q2-d1e8376.summary: Alternatively, before a there is some minimal perceptible time in which he can will, or maximal in which he cannot, in which he should have willed to begin, since obedience requires executing the command's intention, which requires deliberation. So he should will before a to begin at a, and he sinned throughout that time.
claims: Obedience to a command to begin at an instant requires prior deliberate willing.
Omission is sinful throughout the time one should have deliberated.

rh-l1q2-d1e8398.summary: Objection: he omits nothing he should do, since he need do nothing before a. Denied: whoever commands beginning at a commands willing before a to do it; 'I command you to begin willing well at a' would be wholly irrational.
claims: A command to begin includes a command to will beforehand.

rh-l1q2-d1e8418.summary: Reply to the fifteenth: grants that charity might last only an instant; Aristotle means this is impossible when a thing is generated by change in time and corrupted by a natural agent. Reply to the sixteenth: the angel knew God from, not at, the first instant.
claims: Charity might last only an instant.
The angel knew God from, not at, the first instant.

rh-l1q2-d1e8440.summary: Reply to the seventeenth: the argument concludes the opposite, since if the angel sinned only in time, at the extrinsic first instant of that time it was good, in grace. Reply to the eleventh principal argument: denies that a free will would be passive, as in article four. Averroes's dictum is commonly glossed to mean that equal contingency is not found in natural active powers; he does not speak of free active powers.
claims: An angel sinning only in time was good at the extrinsic first instant.
Averroes's dictum concerns natural, not free, active powers.

rh-l1q2-d1e8469.summary: Reply to the twelfth principal argument is deferred to the next question, on the mode of enjoying.

rh-l1q2-d1e8479.summary: Reply to the thirteenth: grants that the will can freely avoid sin, in the sense that before sinning it can freely sin or not, not that it can avoid sin after sinning, as Anselm says the servitude of sin is the inability not to sin.
claims: Before sinning the will can freely sin or not.
According to Anselm, after sinning one cannot avoid that sin.

rh-l1q2-d1e8505.summary: Reply to the Adam argument: each proposition must be distinguished in composite and divided sense. 'It was possible: Adam avoided sin when he sinned' (composite) is false. 'Adam at this time could have avoided sin, and at this time he sinned' (divided) is true, better put as 'Adam, when he sinned, could have avoided sin'. 'He could avoid sin before sinning' is true divided and false composite; the third option is false in both.
claims: When Adam sinned, he could have avoided sin, in the divided sense.
Avoiding sin while sinning is impossible in the composite sense.

rh-l1q2-d1e8551.summary: Objection: take someone now sinning. If he can avoid sin, he is in sin and so cannot avoid it; if he cannot, he does not sin, since by Augustine no one sins in what he cannot avoid.
claims: Present sin seems both avoidable and unavoidable.

rh-l1q2-d1e8571.summary: Reply: 'he sins' and 'he can avoid sin' are incompossible, so pointing to one sinning, he cannot avoid it. Augustine means no one sins by doing what so exceeds his power that he could not avoid it before sinning. One sins because before sinning one could not sin, and the sinner causes his present inability, so it is imputed to him. Further objection: Adam could avoid sin only before time b and always avoided it before b, so did all he could and did not sin; or, if he failed before b, he sinned before b, which is against the case of the first sin.
claims: 'He sins' and 'he can avoid sin' are incompossible.
The sinner is responsible for the inability he causes.

rh-l1q2-d1e8621.summary: Further objection: before Lucifer's fall at a, Michael and Lucifer were equally good, else Lucifer sinned before he sinned. At a Lucifer could not avoid sin, so whenever he could avoid it he did.
claims: Lucifer seems to have avoided sin whenever he could.

rh-l1q2-d1e8646.summary: Reply to the first: denies that Adam could avoid sin only before b, since at b he could avoid it; when he sinned he could have avoided it.
claims: Adam could avoid sin at the time he sinned.

rh-l1q2-d1e8656.summary: Reply to the second: before b he could avoid sinning at b, but it does not follow that he sinned before b. He was not bound before b to avoid sinning at b (which he could not do before b) beyond what he did; at b he was bound to avoid sin at b, and failing that, he first sinned at b.
claims: Adam first sinned at b by failing to avoid sin at b.

rh-l1q2-d1e8682.summary: Reply to the third: grants Michael and Lucifer were equally good up to a, but denies that Lucifer could not avoid sin at a; when he sinned he could have avoided it, in the divided sense.
claims: Lucifer could have avoided sin at the instant he sinned, in the divided sense.

rh-l1q2-d1e8695.summary: Reply to the third form: one cannot avoid a present or future sin as such, but can avoid sin in the divided sense, i.e. can avoid sinning in the future.
claims: One can avoid sinning in the future, not avoid a future sin as such.

rh-l1q2-d1e8708.summary: Reply to the fourth: 'a man can avoid a future sin' is false taken properly, but true taken improperly as 'a man can avoid sinning in the future'.
claims: 'Avoid a future sin' is properly false but true as 'avoid sinning in future'.

rh-l1q2-d1e8724.summary: Reply to the fifth: one is bound to avoid neither a sin one will commit nor one another will commit, but to avoid committing sin.
claims: One is bound to avoid committing sin, not to avoid a determinate future sin.

rh-l1q2-d1e8735.summary: Reply to the sixth, the revelation that only whoever sins tomorrow will be saved, according to the art of obligations. God's revealing a proposition is like positing it, so it must be granted whenever proposed, along with whatever follows formally from it; what follows only as of now is answered as irrelevant, since such consequences are denied in that art.
claims: A revealed proposition functions as a positum in obligational disputation.
Only formal consequences of the positum must be granted.

rh-l1q2-d1e8788.summary: Distinguishes the case. If God posits the revelation while retaining the propositions binding every Christian (to will one's salvation, to will what one believes necessary to it, not to sin mortally), the conjunction is impossible and should not be posited. If God sets aside conflicting propositions and dispenses Socrates from that law, the case is possible: Socrates may not will his salvation, or may will to sin tomorrow without now sinning, since the law is changed and 'whoever wills to sin mortally sins mortally' is deposed. So the inference 'he wills to sin, so he sins' is denied.
claims: Revelation compatible with the common law makes the case impossible.
With divine dispensation from the law, willing to sin tomorrow need not be sin now.

rh-l1q2-d1e8877.summary: Reply to the seventh: God cannot reveal that Socrates will be saved only through murder unless he dispenses from established law, which forbids willing mortal sin and commands willing every necessary means to salvation. God cannot establish contradictories, so the case is not admissible.
claims: God cannot reveal a case contradicting his established law without dispensation.

rh-l1q2-d1e8904.summary: Reply to the eighth: denies outright that one can be necessitated to sin by something external, since whatever one is necessitated to is not imputable as sin, strictly. If someone were necessitated to steal or kill, he should choose stealing and would not sin by stealing.
claims: No one can be necessitated to sin.
What is necessitated is not imputable as sin.
Under necessity, choosing the lesser evil is not sin.

rh-l1q2-d1e8930.summary: Objection: he acts against the precept. Denied: the precept is understood outside necessity, meaning 'you shall not steal spontaneously or voluntarily', since every negative precept prohibits the act of will, not only the exterior act. This answers the canonical authorities. Whether one should sin venially so another avoids mortal sin is left for elsewhere.
claims: Negative precepts prohibit voluntary acts, not acts under necessity.

rh-l1q2-d1e8950.summary: Reply to the ninth: if necessitated to choose between Plato killing Socrates and consenting to Plato's homicide, without other special revelation, he would choose that Plato kill Socrates.
claims: One should prefer suffering death to consenting to murder.

rh-l1q2-d1e8968.summary: Granted that he then consents that Plato sin mortally; it is not always mortal sin to consent that someone sin mortally, and it may even be licit to help someone commit a lesser mortal sin to avoid a greater.
claims: Consenting to another's sin is not always sin.
Helping someone commit a lesser sin to avoid a greater may be licit.

rh-l1q2-d1e8982.summary: Introduces supporting authorities, first Gratian's Decretum, distinction 13.

rh-l1q2-d1e8987.summary: Gratian: no dispensation is admitted against natural law unless two evils press so that one must be chosen; then one should choose the one with lesser obligation. Gregory (Moralia) says the devil's suggestion makes many unable to flee sin without another snare of sin.
claims: According to Gratian, under necessity one should choose the lesser evil.
According to Gregory, some cannot escape one sin without another.

rh-l1q2-d1e9013.summary: The opposite is said by Augustine (De libero arbitrio III.18): if a cause cannot be resisted without sin, yield; if it can, do not. Where deception cannot be avoided at all, there are no sins, for who sins in what can in no way be avoided?
claims: According to Augustine, no one sins in what cannot be avoided.

rh-l1q2-d1e9042.summary: Reply to the tenth, the master and servant: as before, if necessitation is possible, choosing the lesser evil is not sin, while choosing the greater would be.
claims: Choosing the lesser evil under necessity is not sin.

rh-l1q2-d1e9053.summary: Reply to the eleventh, the judge: if the allegations contradict what he certainly knows, he should refer the case to a superior. If he cannot defer or avoid judgment, he must judge according to what is alleged and proved against his own knowledge, since sentencing is only the judicial conclusion of the action before him; the guilt for the injury falls on false plaintiffs and witnesses.
claims: A judge must judge by evidence presented even against private knowledge.
Guilt for unjust judgment falls on false witnesses.

rh-l1q2-d1e9079.summary: Reply to the usury case: in necessity one consents that another commit usury but does not sin, acting to avoid a greater evil, or consents only in a qualified sense. Against this seems Aristotle (Ethics III) on acts done from fear, like jettisoning cargo in a storm, which are voluntary simply, though mixed, since acts are specified by their particular circumstances.
claims: Borrowing at usury in extreme need is not sin.
According to Aristotle, acts under duress are simply voluntary though mixed.

rh-l1q2-d1e9122.summary: Reply to the starving men and one loaf: one should use some stratagem to outwit the other before dying, and is not necessitated to sin.
claims: In the loaf case one is not necessitated to sin.

rh-l1q2-d1e9135.summary: Alternatively, no one may save his life by injuring another. Socrates may take the bread, since in the case it is common to both and he takes what is his, but he may not use violence against his neighbor except to repel force.
claims: One may not save one's life by injuring another.
In extreme necessity the bread is common to both.

rh-l1q2-d1e9153.summary: Objection: one may repel by force someone taking one's cloak, and the bread is mine by necessity. Reply: unlike a cloak, which is personally yours, the bread is yours only in that you may justly take it. Plato has equal right, so his diligence to get it without harming you does you no injury. You may procure it by any means short of injury.
claims: Property by necessity differs from personal property.
Equal claims under necessity exclude violent defense.

rh-l1q2-d1e9189.summary: Changing the case: Plato is nearer or stronger, so Socrates can reach the bread only by killing him. Socrates must save his life and so will the necessary known means, which is killing Plato.
claims: Duty of self-preservation seems to require killing the rival.

rh-l1q2-d1e9207.summary: Further: he must take the bread if he can, but taking it kills Plato as effectively as a sword, since Plato's life depends on it, so he may kill Plato by any means.
claims: Taking the bread kills as effectively as a sword.

rh-l1q2-d1e9220.summary: Further: Plato wants to kill him, and all laws allow self-defense, so he may kill Plato without sin, there being no other defense.
claims: Self-defense permits killing an aggressor.

rh-l1q2-d1e9234.summary: Reply to the first: the inference fails unless the means is licit, which it is not here.
claims: One must will only licit means to self-preservation.

rh-l1q2-d1e9243.summary: Reply to the second: grants antecedent and consequent; one may cause his death one way (taking the bread) but not another, and there is no parity between the just and unjust way.
claims: The same outcome may be licit by one means and illicit by another.

rh-l1q2-d1e9252.summary: Reply to the third: self-defense is licit only against one unjustly trying to take something, which is not the case here. Holcot then adds further proofs that a created will can be necessitated, from two propositions: every created will is intensively finite; and some good or evil makes it so difficult for the will that it cannot will it.
claims: Self-defense applies only against unjust aggression.
A created will is intensively finite.
Some goods or evils are too difficult for the will to will.

rh-l1q2-d1e9276.summary: The first is shown by experience and Anselm: it is much harder to will to enter fire than dew, or to drink gall than water. Anselm says we are sometimes so pressed by temptation that we cannot flee it without difficulty. Since the created will is finite, a temptation can be intensified until it exceeds the will's power of not-willing.
claims: Temptation can be intensified beyond the will's finite resistance.

rh-l1q2-d1e9318.summary: Second: the will can be confirmed in good and obstinate in evil, as every created will in fact will be. The good angel cannot sin, not by nature but by grace (Augustine). If God placed the grace of a blessed mind in a wayfarer of equal power, it would necessitate him to will well too.
claims: Confirmation in grace necessitates good willing.
The grace that confirms the blessed would necessitate a wayfarer too.

rh-l1q2-d1e9353.summary: Third: if God puts a will in the greatest penalty, either it can will it, so that a man in the greatest fire could make it not penal by willing it, or it is necessitated to reject it.
claims: Either the will can neutralize penalty by willing it or it is necessitated to reject it.

rh-l1q2-d1e9374.summary: The first follows from Anselm: nothing is penal unless against the will. If the second, some object necessitates the will to reject it.
claims: According to Anselm, nothing is penal unless against the will.

rh-l1q2-d1e9387.summary: Confirmation: if the will could accept any penalty, it could will eternal damnation and not will beatitude, against Augustine (Enchiridion), who says we will to be happy so that we cannot even will to be miserable.
claims: According to Augustine, we cannot will to be miserable.

rh-l1q2-d1e9407.summary: Fourth: habit diminishes the will's indifference, inclining it in the manner of nature to acts like those that generated it, and more intense habits incline more. Since the will's indifference is finite, some habit would necessitate it, given cognition and other circumstances.
claims: A sufficiently intense habit would necessitate the will.

rh-l1q2-d1e9427.summary: Confirmation from Augustine (Confessions VIII): from perverse will came lust, from serving lust custom, and from unresisted custom necessity. The enemy held his will in a chain; the new will to serve God was not yet able to overcome the old, strengthened by age; flesh and spirit fought, and he suffered unwillingly what he did willingly. The law of sin is the violence of custom, which drags the unwilling mind by its deserved fall.
claims: According to Augustine, unresisted custom becomes necessity.
According to Augustine, the law of sin is the violence of custom.

rh-l1q2-d1e9507.summary: Fifth: one complexion inclines more than another to some object, as the choleric more than the sanguine to revenge. Some degree of intensity can be found at which, with objects and cognition present, the will is carried naturally and without indifference. Experience confirms it: one laboring in summer is necessitated to will to drink, and the hungry cannot freely not desire food.
claims: Bodily complexion can incline the will to necessity.
Hunger and thirst necessitate appetite.

rh-l1q2-d1e9542.summary: Sixth: the magnitude of temptation diminishes guilt. Of two who sin alike, one tempted from outside and one by free choice alone, the second sins more gravely. This is why man's sin was more forgivable than the angel's: man fell by the devil's persuasion, the angel by spontaneous malice.
claims: Temptation diminishes guilt.
Man's sin was more forgivable than the angel's because it was tempted.

rh-l1q2-d1e9565.summary: Seventh: temptation can exceed the will, however firm. Gregory: God mercifully proportions temptations to our strength, for no one bears the snares of the wicked without falling if they exceed the measure.
claims: According to Gregory, temptation beyond one's strength would cause a fall.

rh-l1q2-d1e9591.summary: Reply to the fourteenth principal argument: grants the inference and the consequent. Sorrow is about sin and joy about the sorrow, so they have different objects. Moreover penance is an aggregate of successive acts: one weighs the foulness of sin and ingratitude, judges one should grieve, commands oneself to grieve, then considering the sorrow acceptable to God, rejoices in it after grieving, remembering it, as Augustine says he remembers sadness without being sad. It happens so quickly that one seems to rejoice and grieve at once. Also not every virtuous act is delightful (Ethics III): the brave need only not be saddened.
claims: Penance is an aggregate of successive acts of judgment, sorrow, and joy.
Joy in penance follows sorrow rather than coinciding with it.
Not every virtuous act is delightful.

rh-l1q2-d1e9665.summary: Reply to Anselm's 'nothing voluntary is penal'. Something is voluntary denominatively from a natural volition caused by the will and sensory cognition, which is always the affection for advantage, or from a rational volition caused by discursive cognition, will, and volition. Anselm's major is true in the first sense, and penance is voluntary in the second, so the argument equivocates on 'will'. This ends the question.
claims: Natural volition from sensory cognition differs from rational volition.
Penance is voluntary rationally though penal to the affection for advantage.
